With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Model and actor Chase Mattson has become one of vertical media’s most sought after actors, so when the star was asked to chop it up with the superstars of WWE for ReelShort’s Agent of Shadows, he went all-in, gaining respect for these larger-than-life talents in the process, and telling M&F that he prepares himself for any challenge through serious training and a dedicated attitude to nutrition.

In today’s world, vertical media makes sense. As younger people shun the traditional television and scroll away on social media, the premise of shooting shows vertically allows for seamless viewing on phones. Still, with vertical micro-dramas offering free episodes before a pay wall hides the ending, the pressure to perform to the best of his abilities, for every second, is not lost on Chase Mattson, who was recently named People magazine’s Sexiest ReelShort Star. He’s also become one of the genre’s most able actors.

Mattson’s latest project is titled Agent of Shadows, and is a collaboration between ReelShort and WWE, featuring grapplers such as Drew McIntyre, Booker T, Jacob Fatu, and Nikkita Lyons. And, while Mattson, himself was a highly active athlete in his youth, the 6’3” star was in awe of the likes of McIntyre, who is 6’5.” “I was told that Drew was a big guy and I was like, ‘okay cool, I’m a big guy,’ and then he came on set and this dude is a giant, man!” Fortunately, the star says that he and McIntyre became fast friends.”

Among Mattson’s preferred workouts is the “Cindy” workout, a CrossFit circuit that  Tom Holland has employed to stay in Spider-Man shape. To try it, you’ll perform 5 pullups, 10 pushups, and 15 air squats, then repeat for as many rounds as you can. “I was like, that seems too easy but the first time, I got to round eight, and I was gassed,” shares Mattson. Now, the actor has reached a peak of 16 rounds and is even pushing himself further by squatting with 40-pound dumbbells.

With four kids (and two dogs), Mattson balances family life by embracing the chaos, but with the actor eating five meals per day, you better not touch his bison! Mattson explains that as a model, he simply wasn’t eating enough, but after seeking advice on nutrition, he now tracks his macros, and that means carbs are back in. The star explains that at home, he has his own cupboard for food, meaning that he can stick to his plan in order to stay screen ready.

“We have cabinets in our house, but I have one that us dedicated just for me,” explains Mattson of how he is able to stay focused and avoid the sweet temptations that may be lurking in other areas of the kitchen. The star makes smart swaps, like almonds instead of candy, and eats a large number of blueberries for the effects on muscle recovery. His commitment has certainly paid off, and the actor now weighs in at a lean and muscular 215 pounds as opposed to the 185-pound frame from his modeling days.

Still, when it comes to working out, Mattson often makes it a family affair and shares the fun side of fitness with outdoor jogs and calisthenics, which are great for young bodies.

Not only does he have to stay ripped for the next project, and that could mean just 24-hours’ notice for a shirtless scene, but during the shoot for Agent of Shadows, things got seriously physical. One scene even called for Mattson to mix it up with WWE Hall of Famer Booker T, while filming in the blazing heat of the desert.

“Physically, I was doing all the WWE stunts on the ground,” he explains, noting that his whole body was sore “for days” afterwards.

Mattson went above and beyond with the promotion of this vertical micro-drama too, enrolling at WWE’s Performance Center and stepping inside the ring for real.

“They hit me with a chair, a real chair,” says the actor, reflecting on the surreal nature of his job. “It’s harder than it looks.”

With all of the major streaming platforms now developing, or already offering vertical media, Mattson finds himself as one of the most experienced performers in this area, but as we conclude our conversation, the much sought after star is readying for a flight that will see him working on a regular, horizontal project. Still, in true secret agent style, he can’t tell us anything about it.

“I always stay ready, so I don’t have to get ready,” he signs off.

#8966. Brett Wilkin Shares His Challenging Mass-Building Workout Finishers

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

2024 IFBB Legion Pro winner, and 2025 Mr. Olympia finalist Brett Wilkin is the kind of bodybuilder who leaves it all in the gym. And, in a recent Instagram post, the big man shared the upper and lower body finishers that test his mettle as he looks to pack on even more muscle.

Of course, the aim of any competitive bodybuilder is force their muscle fibers to grow back bigger after being put into a state of hypertrophy from an exhaustive workout, and Wilkin thinks he has found two winning finishers for leveling up his upper and lower body—alternating between supersets and dropsets to approach failure.

Here’s how to try both sequences for yourself.

“Some standing cable flys to failure and straight to the landmine presses,” explained Wilkin to his more than 170,000 Instagram followers. “Stretching it out big to start, then pumping out the inner and upper chest for complete balance. Keeping it simple and effective.”

In the spirit of the superset, Wilkin, who is known to fans as “The Butcher,” takes no rest between the cable fly and landmine press, going big before he goes home. This is a wise combination because the fly hits the shoulders, upper and lower pecs, and even the biceps to some degree, while the landmine two handed chest press has similar coverage but draws upon the triceps more than the biceps.

When it comes to leveraging his lower body, Wilkin opts for drop sets. “Fun fact: Dropsets pair as character builders… and some of y’all out there are lacking character” taunted the man mountain in another recent post.

Setting himself up on the hack squat, Wilkin notes that he rarely observes other gym goers practicing drop sets but explains that they are a go-to for finishing his leg day.

To round out his lower body sessions, the competitive bodybuilder sits low into the hack squat in order to stretch and build his hamstrings and quads. He takes just enough rest time for some plates to be removed before he pounds his pins once again. And, as he works towards failure, Wilkin breathes deeply as he powers through the final moments, readying his legs for even more mass in the future.

“Not just a drop, but tempo work too,” spotted one eagle eyed follower. “Crazy,” wrote another impressed fan. “Big man doing big things!” added yet another.

Ready to build your character in the gym? Be more like Brett Wilkin and try both of these ferocious finishers.

#8965. Studies Show Diet Sodas May Not Be Stalling Weight Loss as Much as Previously Thought

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Artificially sweetened drinks are often demonized based on the theory that they may encourage a greater appetite, or supercharge our sugar cravings, but recent work appears to dispel the bad rap around diet sodas and gaining weight. Now, a two-year clinical trial from the University of Liverpool, England, has provided the greatest insight yet, into the long-term effects of diet drinks on weight loss.

The groundbreaking study, conducted over the course of 104 weeks and published in the British Journal of Nutrition, attempted to build on a similar report in 2023 that also found no proof for the theory that diet sodas can stall weight loss.

While both studies pitted water against zero and low-calorie drinks that were free of sugar (also known as non-nutritive, or NNS beverages) the continued efforts to find the true value of diet drinks is critical, because sugar sweetened beverages often account for a substantial source of dietary sugar, excess calories, and an increased risk of type 2 diabetes. So, if science can show that NNS drinks do not lead to increased sugar intake or excess appetite, they could instead play a part in a balanced diet. To that end, the Liverpool University study has been described as the longest, most comprehensive trial in this area to date. “This study provides the long‑term clinical evidence that has been missing from international discussions,” explained Professor John Halford, who was lead author on the project.

493 overweight or obese adults were entered into a structural weight management program and then split into those who only drank water, and those who consumed a choice of 20 commercially available diet drinks containing aspartame, sucralose, and acesulfame.  Each drink contained less than 2.1 calories per 100ml, with no overall daily calorie cap on drinks. The NNS group were allowed to drink water, but they were asked to drink at least two 330ml servings per day of a diet beverage.

Interestingly, neither group was not blocked from drinking sugary beverages, but they did received coaching to reduce them.

The study also found that overall sugar intake decreased slightly greater in those drinking the NNS beverages, seemingly disproving the theory that artificially sweetened drinks encourage sugar cravings, and suggesting the opposite effect may occur.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomized trial,” said Professor Harrold. “We hope this evidence informs future WHO guidance and public health policy.”

#8964. 5 Yin Yoga Poses for (Practically) Instant Calm

Katie McGrath is a certified yin yoga instructor. She leads classes on her YouTube channel, Yin Yoga with Katie, and offers invaluable advice on YJ as well. Here, she shares five yin yoga poses to help relieve stress so you can find calmness.

Some days bring more stress than others. Perhaps you have stopped (or have yet to start) working yet your jaw is tight, your breath sits high in your chest, and lying down does nothing except give your mind a quiet room in which to be loud.

Yin yoga is useful here for one very practical reason: yin yoga poses hold you close to the ground for several minutes. There is nothing to coordinate and nothing to balance. That combination gives your body and mind—and, more specifically, your nervous system—time to register that you’re in a safe place to release stress, which is something that, depending on you and your circumstances, a faster practice doesn’t always accomplish.

Stay in each of the following yin yoga poses for 3 to 5 minutes—and remember that a longer hold is not necessarily “better.” Aim for roughly 50 to 60 percent of the sensation you could create, which is a line in the sand rather than something carved in stone. If a pose feels exceptionally loud in your body, back off.

As you hold each pose encourage your exhale to become longer than your inhale. This is a simple and effective way to trigger your parasympathetic nervous system. In between the poses, lie flat for about a minute. You can stay still and do nothing or wiggle your body, it’s your choice. That minute is part of the practice, not just a gap in between the poses.

Practicing yoga for stress is not a cure. Instead, it is a way of placing your body in a position where settling down becomes a lot more likely. You might not feel dramatically different, and that is fine. Calm usually feels quieter than we expect it to be. What you are really after is a body that is slightly less braced than it was prior to your practice.

Gather what you have: a bolster or a firm cushion, two blankets, one or two yoga blocks, and a wall. If you have an eye pillow, feel free to use it.

What it does: This is a gentle, fully supported version of Child’s Pose that crosses into restorative yoga, a close cousin of yin yoga. The head makes contact with something solid, which many people find settling on its own. This shape also closes the body inward, which is useful when you want less input rather than more.

How to: Kneel with your knees wide and your big toes touching. Place a bolster lengthways between your thighs and lie your torso down over it. Turn your head to one side. Halfway through your hold, turn it the other way to stretch your neck evenly.

Add more props: Place a block under the far end of the bolster for more support and something solid to rest your head on. If your hips do not reach your heels, add a folded blanket between your calves and your backside, or place a yoga block under your hips. If your knees object to the shape of this pose, lie on your back and hug your knees toward your chest instead. For a more stretch-focused, yin yoga version of this pose, try it without the props.

Hold: Stay here for a total of 4 minutes, two with your head facing each direction.

What it does: This supine twist releases the lower back and the outer hips. And because you are on your back, it asks almost nothing of you but to surrender to gravity.

How to: Lie on your back. Draw both knees toward your chest, then let them fall toward the right. Take your arms out wide. Let your head turn toward the left, if that is comfortable, or keep it neutral as you face the ceiling.

Add props: Place a bolster or folded blanket underneath the knees, if needed, so that they land on something supportive rather than hanging in space. If your right shoulder lifts off the floor, prop it with a folded blanket instead of constantly forcing it toward the mat. If your lower back complains, lower the knees less close to the ground.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: This supported backbend opens your chest and ribcage, which both spend most of the day closed. When the chest is open in Fish Pose, your breath can expand more freely.

How to: Place a yoga block on its lowest level behind you on the mat. For more support, have a second block ready to rest your head on. Lie back onto the block, aligning the bottom of your shoulder blades with one edge. Rest the back of your head on the second block or bring the crown of your head to the mat. Let your arms fall open at your sides. Keep your legs long or you can bend your knees and keep your feet on the mat.

Add props: Add a bolster underneath your knees or, for more of a hip stretch, touch the soles of the feet together and let your knees fall to the sides, tucking cushions underneath your outer thighs. If your lower back is uncomfortable, try lying back over a bolster placed lengthways instead. If your head tips back quite a lot and your throat feels exposed, add a small cushion underneath your head.

Hold: Stay here for 4 minutes. Come out slowly, and rest before you move on.

What it does: This shape offers lateral flexion, also known as a side stretch, which is the direction almost nobody moves during ordinary life. Banana Pose lengthens the body along your outer torso, including the muscles between the ribs, so that your ribcage has more room to expand when you breathe in.

How to: Lie on your back with your legs long. Before you move anything, notice that the backs of both hips are on the floor and level, and try to keep your hips in the center of the mat. Walk both feet to the right, as far as they’ll go without the right hip lifting. Reach your arms overhead and walk both hands toward the right, taking hold of your left wrist with your right hand if that is comfortable and available to you. If you want a more intense side stretch, cross your right ankle over your left. Soften your jaw and let the breath move into the long side of your body.

Add props: No props needed here! Skip the ankle cross if the outer hip is the loudest thing in the pose. If your arms do not want to go overhead, rest them wherever they are comfortable.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: Legs Up the Wall finds the legs are supported and the spine is flat, so it is a good place to stop. It’s also one of the most effective restorative poses for activating your parasympathetic nervous system, allowing for real and accessible relaxation.

How to: Sit sideways with one hip against the wall, then swing your legs up as you lie back. Shuffle your backside close to the wall, or a few inches away if that suits your hamstrings better. Rest your hands on your belly or out to the sides.

Add props: For extra comfort, slide a folded blanket under your hips if your lower back feels flat and strained. If your feet tingle, bend your knees or come down for a moment.

Hold: Stay here for 5-10 minutes or for as long as you need.

Extract yourself from each shape slowly and with care. To finish your practice, find your way to a comfortable seat and breathe here with your eyes closed (or your gaze soft) for 1-3 minutes. Give yourself a moment before you reach for your phone.

#8963. Inside the 24-Hour World Record Attempt That Raised Over $500K+ for a Local Food Bank

Ethan Hunger attempts to break the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons in 24 hours. (Photo: Grayson Baum/Minus 7, Inc)

Beating the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons completed in 24 hours was the goal of my friend Ethan Hunger’s annual community fundraising event. But the record itself was really only a small part of it. The attempt was just one piece of his much bigger, yearlong goal to raise $500,000 for our local food bank – a fundraiser that has been growing through various endurance challenges since 2021.

The idea for his annual “Hunger vs. Hunger” fundraiser was born out of the COVID-related growth of food insecurity in his local area of Bellingham, Washington. What started as a one-year challenge that raised $30,000 has now amassed a total of $1.2 million in donations, and this year’s $500,000 challenge would equate to roughly 7% of the food bank’s annual budget.

The concept and message Ethan shares through these extreme challenges is simple: “No matter how hard a day I create for myself, it will never parallel the struggles of food insecurity.”

For year six, Hunger wanted to go bigger than ever, and a triathlon world record would certainly tick that box while also adding more eyes to the cause. Initially, the record sounded relatively simple when the idea came to light: swim, bike, run, and transition continuously for 24 straight hours – non-stop through the entire night – and beat the previous record of 18 complete triathlons. (Technically, Guinness records the attempt in legs, so he needed 55 completed to surpass the previous record).

However, it quickly became more challenging throughout the buildup. The logistics of putting on a “race” like this at a public park while also adhering to more than 30 pages of Guinness rules began to set in – and that was before considering the largest fundraising goal Hunger had ever attempted.

Here’s how it all unfolded: the behind-the-scenes difficulties of a Guinness World Record, what 24 hours of triathlon actually felt like, how the fundraiser brought it all together, and why he might have stumbled on a revolutionary triathlon idea.

There is a massive difference between saying you broke a world record and having Guinness officially verify it. During the buildup, we found the endless list of verification rules a bit redundant and overly complicated. However, they create a rigorous, no-corner-cutting environment that helps maintain the integrity of the records.

Still, we wished it didn’t cost an estimated $14,000 to send an adjudicator to verify our attempt on-site – which would’ve made everything a lot easier.

Hunger applied for the records six months in advance and was approved. Not everyone gets this approval, as part of the application involves demonstrating that you not only have the experience and skills to attempt something like this, but also the connections and know-how to pull off the necessary verification.

Guinness has a lot of requirements before ratifying an attempt: video, timing, GPS files, logs, photos, and documentation for seemingly everything. So in a feat nothing short of a miracle, we scrambled together seven main cameras to record for 24 hours straight, three additional dedicated cameramen for an upcoming documentary, multiple photographers, timing data, and GPS tracking. But despite all that, one requirement quickly became much more problematic than the others: witnesses.

We discovered late that an individual witness could only cover a four-hour period before needing a four-hour break. We were also further limited in who could qualify, so close friends and family couldn’t simply fill every opening (as we had initially planned).

So, less than a week before a 24-hour event, on top of figuring out nutrition, bikes, course logistics, lights, cameras, batteries, timing, and how the hell any of us planned to stay awake for 24 hours, Ethan now needed to find people willing to stand beside a lake, jump in a safety car for the bike, and on mountain bikes for the run at ridiculous hours of the night and officially confirm that he was, in fact, doing the correct distances.

“If I had to pick one thing that made the event coordination the hardest, it was the witnesses and their four-hour time constraint,” Hunger says.

Somehow, through social media and word of mouth, people volunteered. They came out at midnight, early in the morning, and at all sorts of inconvenient hours. Some of them didn’t know Ethan at all – they simply heard what he was trying to do and wanted to help.

That should have been our first indication of what this event was eventually going to become. The world record might have been Ethan’s, but a lot of people were beginning to feel like they had a small piece of it.

By the end of his record, Hunger had amassed 5.47 miles of swimming, 136.7 miles of biking, and 34.2 miles of running. Yet those numbers are not what he will remember.

I asked him what stands out the most, and his answer goes back to minute one. It paints a picture of the day perfectly:

“The one that lingered for me the longest was likely the starting line. I had been frantically running around for 20 hours trying to get everything set up. I ran over to the start line with my goggles and swim cap, and I looked around with 60 seconds left and finally had the moment sink in of all the incredible people who were there to support me. I saw an older gentleman who I used to volunteer with at the food bank, who I knew had driven 30 minutes to town just to see me start. I saw friends who had flown from around the country. I saw people who currently work at the food bank who came to cheer, and I saw friends who currently rely on the food bank who came to cheer. It was incredibly moving.”

He might have been the one whose name would be attached to the attempt and record, but very quickly it stopped feeling like something he was doing alone. That came partly from the decision to use a real course. From a logistical standpoint, doing the challenge at a pool and track would have been infinitely easier to film, manage, illuminate, and monitor. Every time we left transition on the bike or run course, we disappeared from the main event area, which made everything more complicated.

“There were a ton of moving parts to this, and so many of them were out of my control once the clock started,” Hunger said. “I was able to do my best to get it set up ahead of time and put people in charge of tasks, but then I had to be willing to let it go and hope that it worked out.”

And it did work out: People were joining in on the swim, bike, and run legs throughout almost every reasonable hour (staying behind Ethan to avoid drafting). There was a DJ playing music, food, a campfire, friends sitting around talking, people donating, and strangers coming down simply because they’d heard something ridiculous was happening. Because the distances were short, people could also participate without committing to an enormous endurance challenge of their own. Someone could join one swim, somebody else could do four runs, and others could ride a bunch of the bike legs. Because every leg eventually returned to the same transition area, the group kept coming back together again.

That made the atmosphere completely different from a traditional long-distance triathlon where an athlete might disappear for several hours. If Ethan left on the bike, everyone knew he’d be back in around 25 minutes. If somebody wanted to join the next run, they had a good idea of when it would start.

It helped break the endless cycle of triathlon feeling like such an individual sport and started to feel more like a 24-hour triathlon festival.

We had no idea going in what to expect physically. We’d only practiced this format for about six hours, none of us were truly trained as ultra-triathletes, and sure, we’d completed an Ironman before, but we all safely assumed that somewhere around hour 12 or 15 our bodies would start falling apart.

Weirdly, however, that wasn’t really what happened. Because every individual leg was short and we weren’t moving particularly fast, you’d finish a swim, bike, and run and think, That actually wasn’t too bad. The problem was overcoming the sleep fatigue and the dread of doing specific legs again (and again) with so many hours still ahead.

“My lowest moment was around 3 or 3:30 in the morning,” Ethan says. “I had just finished a triathlon where I was cold the entire time, and I was incredibly sleepy, too. The wind was still causing chop on the lake, and we had headwinds on our bike ride out. I just remember dreading going back in the water because I was already cold, and I knew when I finished the swim, and the wind hit me on the beach, I’d instantly be cold again.”

There were many other smaller obstacles along the way, too. One of which stands out for its irony. Hunger had spent a lot of effort organizing with Outbound Lighting to help illuminate the docks and buoys, to make the night swim one of the coolest parts of the whole experience, yet, in a synchronous moment of shared disbelief, we realized we all had forgotten clear-lens goggles.

On the bike, going from wet to cold to warm meant clothes never quite dried, while chafing, tired hands, wind, darkness, and some sketchy late-night traffic (picture drunk drivers yelling out the window) slowly added up.

Despite that, the hardest part for me might have been the small act of leaving the transition itself: even in the middle of the night, there was a campfire, music, food, and people hanging out, and sitting down beside that fire and prolonging the transition was all too enticing.

Maybe the best way to picture the mental struggle of this challenge is to imagine doing 15 hours of triathlon, getting to 9 a.m. when the sun was finally up, feeling like you’ve survived the hard part – then realizing you still have nine hours left.

For something that had taken 24 hours, the finish felt surprisingly quick. There were lots of people, lots of emotion, and we were all incredibly proud of Ethan. After 22 complete super-sprint triathlons, four more than the previous record, it was finally over.

Then we quickly cleaned everything up and headed to a big party, where Ethan somehow managed to give a speech in front of a few hundred people gathered to celebrate what it was all actually for. The Foodbank.

The number is already over the $500,000 goal, and with still much of the year left, and a documentary release still to come, that should have him far surpassing his expectations.

If you want to donate, you can do so here.

He describes just how much it means to the organization that now helps feed almost 5,000 families weekly in our county:

“My fundraiser is big enough and has been around long enough that the food bank now builds this fundraiser into its annual projection for income. If you combine that with the 2025 federal budget cuts that cost the Bellingham Food Bank around $900,000 and food banks across the country well over $1 billion, the need is there now more than ever.”

There are times when attempting a world record can appear outwardly selfish, done for vanity, to gain attention, or to level up your status. Ethan even received some comments on social media saying so, despite the clear purpose behind the fundraiser. But when you were on-site, you realized there wasn’t much glory in slogging through an attempt like this, and if you dealt with the months of buildup and preparation, you would quickly realize it probably wasn’t worth doing purely for the token of a Guinness stamp.

But doing it for a purpose, and with friends and a community around, made it all worth it. The record gave everyone something ridiculous to rally around; it gave hope, gave purpose, and made every small act feel like it was contributing to something much bigger.

Speaking of bigger, Ethan has already planned next year’s challenge: a 100-mile run around our local track and stadium.

#8962. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

#8961. 7-Minute Yoga to Practice While Sitting at Your Desk

Yoga while sitting at your desk can be a simple way to soothe physical tension during the work day. This practice was created by instructor Laia Bové, who has taught students of all levels for more than a decade.

If you spend a lot of time hunched over your desk, you already know that it’s important to break the stagnation of long hours in front of your computer screen. But sometimes the time you think you’ll have to release the tension in your neck, shoulders, and upper back—likely before or after work—disappears due to other responsibilities, distractions, or just plain exhaustion.

This 7-minute yoga practice was made with the idea that you can sneak in a little yoga during work. These stretches target the most common areas where tension and aches arise when sitting at a desk and act as a quick reset. By the end of the seven minutes, you’ll feel a lot looser throughout your upper back and maybe even a little more ready to take on the rest of your day.

You can do this sequence between tasks, meetings, or calls, or after you power off your laptop and before you move on to other activities. You don’t need any special clothes or equipment—in fact, you don’t even need to get up from your chair.

Sit in your desk chair with your feet planted on the floor. Exhale and lower your chin toward your chest. Inhale and lift your chin toward the ceiling. Repeat that a few times.

Next time you exhale and lower your chin toward your chest, keep your chin lowered as you turn your head toward the right, as if you were drawing your nose toward your right shoulder. Take a breath here, then return to center with your chin still lowered. Then draw your nose toward your left shoulder. Return to center, then lift your chin to neutral.

Clasp your hands and rest them lightly behind your head. Point your elbows toward the sides of the room to prevent your hands from placing too much pressure on your head. Inhale as you lift your chest and draw your elbows slightly behind your chest, if possible, and slightly arch your back in a Cow Pose variation.

Keeping your hands where they are, exhale as you round your back, bring your elbows toward each other, and draw your navel toward your spine in a seated variation of Cat Pose. Repeat another round of this seated Cat-Cow variation.

Keeping your hands clasped behind your head, exhale as you lean toward the left, feeling a stretch along your right side. Inhale and return to center. Exhale as you bend toward the right, feeling a stretch along your left side. Inhale and return to center, then release your arms.

Place your fingertips on your shoulders and point your elbows toward the sides of the room. Draw your elbows toward each other in front of your chest as if you want them to touch, then lift them to point toward the ceiling, then point them toward the back wall, and then point them at the floor, moving in a large circular motion. Continue drawing elbow circles as many times as you like. Then switch directions.

Exhale and tilt your head toward the right, drawing your right ear toward your right shoulder. Inhale and return to center. Exhale and tilt your head toward the left, drawing your left ear toward your left shoulder. Repeat a few times.

Reach your arms out to your sides in a T shape, then cross your arms and wrap them around your chest as if you’re giving yourself a big hug. Take a few breaths here in Eagle Arms variation. Then repeat with the opposite arm on top. Release your arms.

With your arms relaxed at your sides, draw your shoulders up toward your ears and squeeze your muscles as tightly as you can—maybe you even scrunch the muscles in your face. Take a big breath in, then release your shoulders down and relax the muscles you were tightening. Repeat one more Shoulder Squeeze.

Take a big breath in through your nose and out through your mouth. Repeat as many times as needed until you’re ready to resume your day.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#8959. How Yin Yoga Bananasana Can Transform Your Swimming

Swimmers spend plenty of time working on stroke mechanics and building upper-body strength, but mobility of the side body, particularly the intercostal muscles between the ribs, can affect how freely you can breathe, especially as fatigue sets in.

Bananasana, a gentle yin yoga pose, stretches the side body. A supported side-lying pose, with blocks under the ribs and head, creates a more targeted stretch that can help expand your ribs for three-dimensional breathing.

While Bananasana offers a relatively subtle lateral stretch of the obliques, intercostal muscles, and IT band, a supported side-lying variation increases the sensation and may help ease fascial tightness.

Fascia is a network of connective tissue that surrounds and connects muscles, nerves, bones, and organs. When fascia’s layers glide well, the body moves freely. However, training load, injury, prolonged postures, and other factors can contribute to stiffness or reduced mobility. Restriction in the rib cage and side body can make a full, expansive breath feel harder to achieve.

Give your shoulders and lats attention, but don’t overlook your ribs and side body. Add these stretches to your regular mobility routine to build breath awareness and find more ease and efficiency in the water.

#8958. I Wish Yoga Studios Would Stop Trying to Sell Me on Their Teacher Training Programs

Los Angeles-based yoga instructor Ramoni Overton questions whether a common trend across yoga studios is negatively affecting students. Overton is the creator of the YouTube channel Yoga With Ramoni.

I was brand new to yoga when I first experienced a teacher training sales pitch at the end of class. I had stood up after Savasana feeling pure bliss, practically floating off my mat. But suddenly the instructor was pedaling the studio’s upcoming yoga teacher training (YTT) to the entire room. I was surprised, but I mostly brushed it off, assuming it was a one-time thing.

But then it happened a second time. Then a third. And a fifth. After I heard the exact same sales pitch multiple times, my post-class high vanished before I even made it to the front door. It was replaced by a single thought. “Seriously? Again?”

This experience isn’t unique to me—it’s been happening to many other yoga students. And, in my opinion, it’s a reason why some of them might quietly not return to class.

As a yoga teacher for four years and a yoga student for nine, I’ve noticed that most students aren’t coming to yoga to build a second career. They already have full days and packed schedules. They’re coming to yoga to unwind, decompress, and experience a single hour in which the outside world completely disappears.

At the same time, I understand the reasons behind the post-class YTT pitch. Yoga studios have bills to pay, and YTT is one of the more reliable revenue streams in a business that runs on thin margins. But when studios push their instructors to pitch constantly (and when some instructors receive commission for every sign-up), the pressure is on. The yoga teacher who was supposed to hold space for you is now knowingly or unknowingly working a sales quota. That changes the energy of a studio, whether anyone admits it or not.

And it adds up to something that’s bigger than one annoying moment. Seemingly everywhere else in life, we are constantly being sold something. Ads interrupt us while we’re watching TV, listening to podcasts or the radio, and scrolling through social media. Yoga was supposed to be one of the few places that wasn’t also a marketing funnel.

Studios don’t need to stop sharing information about their YTT offerings. But they do need to stop treating every student on the mat as a sales lead. There are so many ways to share training info without disrupting the post-class quiet. A simple flyer at the front desk, an announcement on the studio schedule, or a free information session for those who are genuinely curious. Let people come, flow, and leave in peace.

If the training is enticing, students will ask about it on their own. You won’t have to sell them on it.

#8957. Transform Your Core with This 10-Minute Exercise Ball Workout

An exercise (or stability) ball is an inexpensive but effective strength training tool for triathletes. (Photo: Getty Images)

For this article, retired pro triathlete and Triathlete contributor Emma-Kate Lidbury spoke to strength coach and former pro Dede Griesbauer about why this stability ball workout is so effective for triathletes.

Here’s the thing about strength training for triathletes: Almost nobody skips it because they don’t believe in it. They skip it because of the drive to the gym or the 90 minutes that don’t exist between that threshold bike workout and school pickup.

So what if we make life a little easier and remove some of the barriers to getting strength done?

This routine does exactly that and requires one piece of equipment – an exercise ball – and a patch of floor about the size of a yoga mat. No need for dumbbells, a bench, a gym membership, or the drive there. You can pick up an exercise ball for about the same price as a mid-range pair of goggles; it can fit into most any suitcase; and it might just help you find every stabilizer muscle you’ve quietly neglected since your last off-season strength block.

A stability ball is, by design, unstable. That’s the entire value proposition. It offers the following benefits:

Every exercise here demands you hold a neutral spine against something actively trying to move you out of it. Former pro triathlete turned strength coach Dede Griesbauer points out that this pays off in two places triathletes care about: run efficiency, and the ability to hold a stable position in the aerobars.

With an exercise like the rear foot elevated lunge (below), Griesbauer notes this forces each leg to work independently, which may reveal the left-right discrepancies a bilateral squat lets you hide. This matters for power balance on the bike and for not favoring one side on the run, which can help reduce injury risk.

Almost every movement in this routine trains multiple muscle groups at once. Griesbauer’s summary: It offers good “bang for the buck” with minimal equipment, minimal space, and minimal setup.

Griesbauer advises adding strength work to your hard days, not because it’s pleasant to stack lifting onto a threshold run, but because the alternative – sprinkling it across easy days – erodes the recovery that those days are designed to deliver.

“Make your hard days hard so that your easy days can be easy,” she says.

That’s the ideal. Griesbauer is also clear about what “ideal” might look like for an age-grouper with a job.

“Not everyone will have time to do their hard bike or run session AND make time for strength on the same day,” she says. “The good news is that this session isn’t heavy loading. These are good basic movements, so if you are time-crunched, adding them wherever you can is better than not doing them at all.”

Two sessions a week is the target, but once isn’t a failure. “Some is better than none,” Griesbauer says, “so if you can only do it once? Get it done once.”

Start with a single pass through all nine exercises (which should take approximately 10-12 minutes).

Once one round stops feeling like work, add a second. Then, if time allows, add a third. Three circuits should take you about 30-35 minutes and is plenty of stimulus for a routine that isn’t loading you heavily. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between exercises and a couple of minutes between rounds.

Progress through the workout in the order listed. It moves between lower body, core, and upper body so nothing fatigues to failure.

Stand on your right foot with your left leg extended behind you and the top of your left foot resting on the ball. Bend your right knee until your right thigh is parallel to the floor, keeping your torso upright and your weight on your heel. Now press your heel into the floor and return to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions and then repeat the exercise with your left leg.

Begin in a prone position with the tops of your feet resting on the ball, your palms on the floor underneath your shoulders, and your body forming a straight line. Now contract your stomach muscles, bend your knees, and roll the ball toward your chest. Pause briefly and roll the ball back until your body forms a straight line again. Complete 12 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your feet together, your body forming a perfectly straight line and your palms positioned slightly more than shoulder-width apart on the ball. Bend your elbows and smoothly lower your chest to within an inch of the ball. Immediately press back upward to the start position. If you have difficulty doing a full push-up, do a half push-up, bending your elbows only to 90 degrees before pressing upward. Complete 10 repetitions.

Start in a bridge position, face up, with your head and shoulders on the floor and your heels resting on top of the ball, your body suspended in a straight line between these points. Contract your hamstrings and roll the ball toward your butt. Pause briefly and extend your legs, rolling the ball back to the starting point. Don’t let your hips drop. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, elevating one foot above the ball and pulling the ball toward your butt with the other leg.

Kneel on the floor facing the ball, lean forward slightly, and place your forearms on top of the ball. Pull your belly button toward your spine. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your forearms out in front of you and allowing your body to tilt toward the floor. Concentrate on maintaining perfect alignment of your spine. Stop just before you’re forced to arch your back. Hold this position for a two-count and then return to the start position, exhaling as you do so. Complete 12 repetitions.

Lie facedown on the ball with your palms on the floor. Begin with the ball supporting your pelvic area. Now use your hands to drag your body forward over the ball until it is underneath the tops of your feet, keeping your body in a straight line. Pause briefly and roll back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your palms on the floor, the tops of your feet resting on the ball, and your body in a perfectly straight line between them. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Go as far as you can without strain; it’s OK if it isn’t very far. Now press back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Lie face up with your upper back supported by the ball, your feet flat on the floor about 12 inches apart, your knees bent and your body forming a “tabletop” from knees to chest. Contract your calf muscles and raise your heels off the floor without allowing your hips to sag. Now lower your heels back to the floor. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, first crossing your left ankle over your right knee and then doing the reverse.

Get into a plank position with your palms on the floor underneath your chest and the ball supporting your shins. Keeping your arms straight, press the heels of your palms into the floor and push your body backward so that the ball rolls up under your thighs. Go as far as you can and then pull your body in the opposite direction until you’re back in the start position. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, start with the ball under the tops of your feet.

Instability is the point, which also means this routine isn’t universally appropriate. Griesbauer flags a few pointers worth knowing before you start. Note that none of these are a reason not to train. They just require you to adapt or swap movements if needed.

If you have a cranky lower back: The abdominal rollout generates high spinal extension and shear force if your core gives out mid-rep, which can be a genuine problem for anyone with disc history. The reverse crunch can pull you into loaded lumbar flexion if control slips, and a hamstring curl performed with dropped hips will arch and cramp the low back.

If you have “shoulder history”: Push-ups on a moving ball tax the rotator cuff hard, and the ball walk-out places prolonged, shifting load on the shoulder joint. Skip both if you’ve dealt with instability or impingement.

If you have wrist issues: The ball’s spherical surface forces the wrists into deep extension while the weight moves under you. Elevated push-ups shift more bodyweight forward onto the same joints.

If you have knees and hip flexor problems: The rear foot elevated lunge loads the front knee in deep flexion and stretches the trailing leg aggressively, which can be enough to tip the pelvis if your hip flexors are tight. Tight hip flexors will also hijack the reverse crunch from the lower abs.

If you have cramp-prone calves and hamstrings: The bridge heel raise fires the calves while the hamstrings are already shortened, which is a reliable spasm trigger. The hamstring curl frequently cramps athletes with weak hamstrings on the concentric.

If you have compromised balance: Any single-leg work raises fall risk. Have a wall or chair within reach if you feel you might need it.

#8956. 4 Things You’re Doing in Yoga That Might Worsen Lower Back Discomfort

Monica Bright is a yoga teacher whose continuing education centered on injury mechanics and movement. She breaks down the common yoga mistakes that could be worsening lower back discomfort, and offers options for relief. You can also learn more about yoga poses for your lower back.

Lower back discomfort is one of the most common pain points among people worldwide. If you fall into that category and also do yoga, chances are you’ve expected the practice to bring you relief. But certain movements in yoga, and how you approach them, can sometimes have the opposite effect of the lower back release that you were hoping to achieve.

Learning to recognize what triggers tightness in your lower back can help you make more supportive choices on and off the mat. That way, you’re still working toward undoing your discomfort, but without accidentally worsening it.

Whether you’re in class or at home, or even moving throughout your everyday life, notice whether any of the following approaches to movement worsens your lower back sensitivity—and explore the following alternatives that might help relieve your discomfort.

Some people’s lower back strain is aggravated by moving too quickly. This is often the case with forward rounding. Think Seated Forward Bend or reaching down to pick something up off the floor. Moving slowly allows you to pay attention to the sensations in your body and ensures you’re not accidentally forcing yourself to move too far into a stretch and tweak your lower back.

What to try instead: Throughout your yoga practice, and even during your day, ask yourself, “How does it feel when I move more slowly?”

The “neutral” position of your spine that you commonly hear yoga teachers mention includes several curves, including one in the lumbar spine that is concave, meaning it curves inward. But many students have a tendency to round the lower back during certain poses, such as forward bends and Chair Pose, which can have the effect of flattening the lower spine and causing tension.

What to try instead: Maintaining that neutral spine can be more beneficial than “flattening” it for some students with a track record of stiffness and soreness in the lower back. That comes into play in several common yoga poses.

In Chair Pose, for instance, there is a tendency to draw the core toward the spine so much that it counteracts the natural curve in the lower back. Maintaining a neutral spine means keeping the length in your lower back rather than tucking the tailbone.

In Standing Forward Bend, keeping a neutral spine means being aware if you are rounding your lower back as you reach forward and, instead, hinging at your hips, perhaps bending your knees, and not being concerned with how far forward you fold.

However, some students find a greater sense of ease in the lower back by rounding forward. Ask yourself, “Does my lower back feel better, or worse, with rounded forward folds?”

If your lower back is sensitive, your yoga practice might look different from the person’s on the mat next to you—and that’s okay. The goal in yoga isn’t to push past discomfort, but to find the alignment in which your lower back feels good. And sometimes that means taking variations.

What to try instead: Explore variations of poses—some of which might include using props, such as blocks—to help support your movements. Take Happy Baby, for example. Drawing your knees toward your chest and holding the backs of your thighs might feel more supportive to some. When sitting in a forward bend, placing a blanket underneath the lowest part of your back to slightly elevate your hips and provide more room for your lower back might be your preferred version. Finding the movement options that feel tolerable for you can be enormously helpful while you’re learning to prioritize your lower back.

Stress, poor sleep, a sense of being overwhelmed, even anxiety surrounding practicing certain movements can put your body on high alert and cause your nervous system to brace for impact. This has the potential to turn up the volume on physical discomfort. Understanding how to downregulate your nervous system, on the other hand, can help your entire body relax.

What to try instead: You’re likely familiar with some of the practices that activate your parasympathetic nervous system, including resting in poses such as Child’s Pose, Legs Up the Wall, or Crocodile and practicing various pranayama (breathwork) techniques, including Box Breathing or simply lengthening your exhalations. Even slowing the pace of your practice and taking the variations that feel good to you are ways of signaling to your nervous system that you’re safe. Experiment with one or two calming exercises prior to your next yoga class or at-home practice.

Practicing with these ideas in mind will ultimately help you recognize how to support your body when practicing yoga. This doesn’t mean you need to have to have all of the answers. It simply, but it does means that you are present, aware, and listening to your own body’s signals.
