#8955. Post-Race Weight Gain: Why You’re Heavier After Finishing a Race (And Why It’s a Good Thing)

You wake up feeling sore and puffy the day after a race, step on the scale, and confirm what you intuitively feel: you’re a few pounds above your pre-race weight.

But why? Logically, a massive calorie burn (up to 10,000+ calories for an Ironman!) should tip the scale the other way, so something must be wrong.

Your first impulse may be to cut calories or jump right back into training. Please don’t! What you’re seeing is your body’s normal physiological response as it goes into full recovery mode.

Post-race weight gain isn’t the same as the off-season weight drift many athletes experience. That weight tends to build over months and is a separate conversation about energy balance. The jump you see on the scale in the first 24 to 72 hours after the race is mostly water. Specifically, your body is hard at work replenishing glycogen, rebuilding plasma volume, and retaining water and sodium as part of its hormonal stress-and-repair response. It’s most noticeable after a half or full iron-distance triathlon, where fueling, fluid intake, and stress load are highest.

Let’s dig into what’s going on, and why this temporary bump is actually a good sign.

Long-course races drain your muscle glycogen. As long as you eat plenty of carbs, your body starts refilling those stores within the first few hours after you finish. But the longer the race, the more muscle damage, which slows the process.

After a long-course race, full restoration can take several days, rather than the roughly 24 hours we see after shorter events. Here’s the kicker: each gram of newly synthesized glycogen is stored with approximately three grams of water. So, replenishing 400–500 grams of muscle glycogen adds about 3.5–4.5 pounds, mostly from water, packed in your muscles. In other words, much of the bump you see on the scale in the first few days is restored fuel.

Glycogen isn’t the only reason the scale climbs. It’s normal to finish a long race dehydrated, since even a solid race hydration strategy can’t fully offset hours of sweat losses. In the 24 to 72 hours after the race, fluid-conserving hormones (aldosterone and vasopressin) remain elevated, signaling your body to hold onto fluid to restore plasma volume and electrolyte balance. The extra water weight won’t stick around long, so don’t cut back on fluids or salt to bring the number down. Your body needs both right now.

Racing 70.3 or 140.6 miles puts your body under more stress than a typical training day. During and after the race, cortisol, your primary stress hormone, spikes, signaling your body to retain water. Prolonged physical exertion causes muscle microdamage and inflammation.

The longer, hotter, and tougher the race, the longer recovery may take. As your body begins repairs, fluid moves into damaged tissues, which can explain your tight, swollen legs. You’ll notice improvement when your kidneys start clearing the excess fluid, leading to more frequent bathroom visits. A little puffiness for a couple of days post-race means the repair process is underway.

As training volume comes down after a race, you might expect your appetite to follow. And, for the first several hours, it often does, since hard effort can temporarily suppress hunger. But over the next day or two, it returns with a vengeance. That’s because a slower-moving hormonal system (primarily ghrelin and leptin) signals your brain to respond to the energy deficit you built up on race day.

You may feel hungrier for several days, often craving energy-dense, salty, carb-rich foods (think fries, burgers, and pizza). And all that yummy food, along with the water and sodium that come with it, adds to the scale number too. It’s not a lack of willpower or a total loss of control; it’s your body refueling.

Following an endurance race, some swelling is expected, but I’d be remiss not to flag a few scenarios that, although rare, require medical attention.

If one leg swells, especially with calf pain, warmth, or redness, it may indicate a blood clot. Swelling with shortness of breath or chest pain is an emergency; seek immediate attention.

Dark cola-colored urine with severe muscle pain or weakness could signal rhabdomyolysis: a condition involving severe muscle breakdown that can lead to kidney damage.

And if you finish the race heavier than you started and experience confusion, headache, or nausea, it could be hyponatremia (low blood sodium); seek medical help right away.

For most athletes, a few extra pounds in the days after a long-distance race signals a healthy recovery. Still, it can be tempting, especially if you keep close tabs on your weight, to see the number go up and immediately want to cut back or restrict.

Resist the urge. Your body needs carbohydrates and protein to rebuild glycogen and repair tissue; your fluid and electrolyte balance needs restoring, and your immune system needs adequate energy while under duress. Restricting food and fluids now won’t get your weight back on track. It will delay glycogen restoration, prolong fatigue and soreness, and potentially increase your risk of illness.

As your fluid levels normalize and inflammation subsides, most of the extra weight comes off naturally, typically within three to seven days. You’ve demanded a lot from your body in training and on race day, so give it what it needs: plenty of nutrient-rich food, adequate hydration, rest, and quality sleep. Then step back and trust your body and the process.

#8953. Locust Pose Might Be a Simple Backbend, But It Can Help Improve Your Posture

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the backbend Locust Pose first appeared in the July-August 1996 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

If a picture is worth a thousand words, then our posture speaks volumes. Poor carriage of the torso—rounded shoulders, sunken chest, and a downward cast of the eyes—generally suggests a negative state of being. Good posture, on the other hand—shoulders rolled back and down, chest lifted, and an energetic carriage—demonstrates confidence and a sense of purpose.

All the backbending yoga postures help create this physical expression of assurance. You feel better, have more energy, and benefit from an enhanced respiratory system. The internal alignment of the organs is refined as we adjust and improve the external alignment.

The postures actually have the potential to positively and profoundly affect you on all levels: physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual. Approaching your asanas with this awareness is the key to the enrichment of your practice.

The repertoire of backbending postures, or hyperextensions of the spine, is vast. In this article, we are going to focus on one of the more basic back-bending poses, Grasshopper or Locust Pose (Salabhasana). There are several variations of this posture, according to different systems or styles of hatha yoga. We will practice two versions of Locust, beginning with Salabhasana One as described in B.K.S. Iyengar’s Light on Yoga.

Locust is excellent for correcting poor posture, as well as for counteracting the development of kyphosis, the rounding of the upper back. It tones the whole posterior of the body, strengthens the abdominals, and enhances digestion.

Begin by lying face down on your mat, with your arms at your sides near your hips, palms facing upward. Tuck your chin in, forehead on the floor.

Engage your abdominals by drawing your navel in and up, to stabilize your lower back. Contract your buttocks and quadriceps. Keep the knees, legs, and feet together. Exhale the breath as you simultaneously raise the head, chest, arms, and legs. Look forward and up. Hold and breathe for five to 10 seconds. Keep the abdominals firm so you feel the support from underneath.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position. Turn your head to the side and completely relax. Repeat once or twice more.

Full Locust begins in the same base position, but with the arms outstretched at shoulder level, perpendicular to the body. The palms are facing down, and the chin is on the mat. The knees, legs, and feet are together.

Engage your abdominal muscles by drawing your navel in and up; contract your buttocks and quadriceps. This time, inhale the breath as you raise the arms, chest, head, and legs. Look forward and up. Breathe naturally as you hold the posture for five to 10 seconds. Keep your shoulders away from your earlobes as you continue to stretch your arms back and slightly upward. Palms remain facing the floor. The idea is to lift the entire body upward as you balance on the center of your abdomen.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position, and relax. Repeat once or twice more.

If your lower back is sensitive or you are prone to chronic neck tension, you may want to practice the pose in the following stages.

Lie on your stomach, face down, arms at your sides near your hips. Palms are facing up, the chin is tucked in, and the forehead is on the floor. Legs are hip-distance apart. Firm the buttocks and abdominals as well as the quadriceps.

Inhale the breath. Exhaling, raise just the arms to about hip level, keeping the palms facing up. The head remains on the floor. Lengthen the neck and focus on strengthening your back muscles. Feel your shoulder blades pull down your back and slightly together.

Keep the abdominals, buttocks, and legs firm. Exhale and lower down.

Next, repeat what you’ve just done and add the lifting of the chest. The neck and head will come up as well, but keep looking downward so the neck remains extended rather than arched. Inhale in your base position. Exhale and raise the arms only. Inhale and hold. Ex-haling, raise the chest. Again, hold and breathe rhythmically for five to 10 seconds. Exhale as you lower down.

In the same beginning position, inhale the breath, and exhale raising the arms up. Hold and inhale. Exhale, raising the chest. Hold and inhale. Finally, exhale and raise the legs. Hold and breathe. Keep looking at the floor, focusing on lengthening the body from the top of your head to your fingertips on down to your toes. When you’re ready, lower down on an exhalation. Turn your head to the side, release the pose completely, and relax.

A natural inclination after performing a back bend is to pull your knees to your chest. So after your last repetition, you may want to got into Child’s Pose: Kneel back onto your heels, folding your torso over your thighs with your head resting on the floor in front of your knees. Arms are at your sides with palms facing up.

If your head doesn’t rest on the floor easily, simply fold your arms underneath your forehead for support.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8950. The Science of “Extreme” Exercise During Pregnancy

The author attended the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto to hear directly from Margie Davenport and Michelle Mottola, key researchers shaping the upcoming 2027 International Olympic Committee guidelines. The resulting piece analyzes their latest clinical and survey data on pregnant athletes engaging in heavy weightlifting, high-intensity intervals, endurance sports, and rock climbing.

Back in 2019, I wrote about a new set of guidelines for exercise during pregnancy. These guidelines were revolutionary—up to a point. Advice from doctors at the time was often extremely conservative, like never letting your heart rate exceed 140 beats per minute. But solid evidence now suggested that consistent moderate exercise—at least 150 minutes spread over at least three days per week—was not just safe for most pregnant women but was actually beneficial for both mother and fetus, dramatically lowering the risk of conditions such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and depression.

Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more!

Beyond that threshold, though, the deadlines dared not tread. Moderate exercise? Sure. Lifting heavy weights, or running marathons, or going rock climbing? That’s a trickier question, because no scientist wants to send a pregnant person out to do something that could potentially harm her or her baby. But ignoring it doesn’t make sense, because many female athletes do continue participating in their sports while pregnant, regardless of what the guidelines say. And those who stop or dramatically reduce their activity may suffer declines in both physical and mental health.

It’s important, then, to understand what the evidence says about the risks and benefits of more extreme forms of exercise. In 2018, the answer was “not much.” But in the years since then, there has been a steady flow of research on pregnant athletes doing hard things. In fact, the International Olympic Committee is planning to release a new and dramatically revised set of guidelines for pregnant athletes in 2027.

At the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto last week, I had a chance to hear two key authors of both the old and new guidelines—Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University—speak about their research. They couldn’t yet reveal what’s in the new guidelines, but they did share some of the key research that informs them. Here are some highlights from the extreme frontiers of exercise and pregnancy.

Any sort of heavy lifting is frowned upon during pregnancy, and particularly lifting while lying on your back, which could compress key blood vessels. But this advice, Davenport points out, is based on expert opinion and workplace studies, where heavy lifting is different from lifting in the gym where you control load and recovery.

To start, she and her colleagues surveyed 679 recreational weightlifters and CrossFit athletes who were pregnant and habitually lifted at least 80 percent of their one-rep max. Those who continued heavy lifting had a 51 percent reduction in complications compared to those who obeyed the guidelines and dialed back their training. They were also roughly half as likely as normal to report postpartum depression after delivery.

Of course, survey studies have limitations: maybe complications caused people to stop lifting rather than the other way around, for example. But those initial positive results paved the way for bringing 10 pregnant women into the lab and having them do squats, bench press, and deadlift for 10 reps at up to 90 percent of 10-rep max. They monitored maternal and fetal heart rate, umbilical blood pressure, glucose and lactate levels, and various other health markers, and compared the results to those of ten non-pregnant controls; there were no causes for concern.

A heart-rate limit of 140 is outdated. Still, the 2019 guidelines remain cautious. “Vigorous” exercise, they suggest, should top out at around 169 beats per minute for women 29 and younger, and 162 beats per minute for those 30 and older.

In a 2023 study, Davenport and her colleagues put that ceiling to the test. They had 15 volunteers, at an average of 27 weeks pregnant, do either a 30-minute moderate bike ride or 10 x 1:00 intervals at above 90 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate. The women ended up reaching a peak of 96 percent on average during the intervals, with some getting as high as 105 percent of max. (This isn’t Spinal Tap: the standard estimate of max heart rate, 220 minus age, was clearly off for these women.)

Once again, the researchers took a bunch of measures of fetal and maternal physiological responses. There were no relevant differences between the moderate and intense exercise sessions.

This was another survey study: 331 women who, on average, were 33.2 years old and had completed 2.1 pregnancies. All had engaged in exercise bouts lasting at least an hour during their pregnancies; 80 percent had continued long-duration exercise throughout their pregnancies, but in most cases had gradually decreased overall training as the pregnancy progressed.

Davenport and her colleagues divided the respondents into two subgroups: those who continued to do at least 300 minutes of exercise per week during their third trimester, and those who were below that threshold. Those in the high exercise group had a lower risk of complications during delivery, but a higher risk of diastasis recti—a separation of the stomach muscles—after delivery.

The overall conclusion was that long-duration exercise well above guideline recommendations “appears to be well tolerated” by people who are already used to that level of training.

Here’s where things get interesting, because it’s hard to wave away the hypothetical dangers of a hard fall. But do these risks justify telling people not to climb?

Davenport has led a couple of studies exploring this issue. One involved interviewing 11 elite climbers who continued to train or compete during pregnancy about their perspectives on risk. Climbing, one of the climbers said, was actually safer than walking down the street: “I’m less likely to fall because I’ve got three points of contact on, compared to one when I’m walking… So I feel like I’m more likely to trip over something in the dark on the street than falling while climbing up a climbing wall.”

The second study surveyed nearly 700 climbers who had climbed through pregnancy, logging a cumulative total of 64,000 hours of climbing and suffering 155 self-diagnosed “hard falls.” Here there were two adverse events (one vaginal bleeding, the other undeclared), but both births were healthy. Climbing isn’t without risks, Davenport says, but the findings suggest the risks are lower than previously thought. Of note, 96 percent of respondents were “happy” or “very happy” they had continued to climb.

There’s more—Davenport has also studied contact sports like soccer, for example—but you get the picture. Some of these activities clearly involve theoretical risks, but those theoretical risks need to be balanced against the measurable mental and physical benefits of continuing to train and the risks of stopping. One of the best predictors of post-pregnancy injury, for example, is having reduced your training by more than 50 percent during pregnancy.

The focus of the upcoming IOC guidelines will be “athlete-centered decision-making”—not an ironclad set of rules about who can do which types of exercise when, but a framework about how to weigh the pros and cons in different contexts. It’s an important update, because it recognizes what’s already happening in the real world. “Our current public health guidance is fantastic and sets our baseline,” Davenport says. “But most athletes—well, all athletes—are going to vastly exceed current recommendations.”

For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

#8949. These Are the Three Accessories You Need for a New Bike—And the One You Don’t

The right accessories can make your first rides safer, smoother, and more fun.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

During my time working in bike shops, I have sold hundreds, if not over a thousand, bikes, and significantly more accessories. I’ve seen some people buy every accessory under the sun while they get their new bike, and others opt out of any accessories other than a bottle cage. A bottle cage is a good start, but there are a few other accessories to make sure you have the best possible first ride.

New bike day is a big day. The price of a new bike from a name brand manufacturer can be a big expense, so it’s understandable to hesitate when having to buy more. However, I’ve seen too many bikes become a clothes rack in a basement because someone didn’t have the experience they were hoping for on those first crucial rides. Getting the right gear from day one can change those initial impressions from negative to positive, but be aware you don’t need to buy all the things at once.

Here we’ll talk about the three accessories I recommend on day one, the one accessory I’ve steered a lot of riders away from when getting a new bike, and a few honorable mentions to consider as you ride more. Whether you’re a seasoned rider or just looking for tips on your first bike purchase, this story is for you.

Assuming you’re buying a bike that comes with pedals, helmets have always been the first piece of gear I suggest to riders buying a new bike. While helmets are not foolproof, they are a significant line of defense in keeping you safe as a rider. I’ve personally broken five helmets over the years, one of those times the doctor told me it likely saved my life. Keep in mind you don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars on a great helmet. When considering a new helmet, Virginia Tech Helmet Rating is the go-to resource on helmet safety testing.

Tara Seplavy, deputy editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on some of the Bicycling team’s favorite picks from the top-rated Virginia Tech helmets. One of the highest value helmets from the top ten on the Virginia Tech list is the P2R A20 Mips. This helmet comes in at only $60. “With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price,” says Seplavy.

If you’re buying your fifth bike and think you don’t need a new helmet, consider this—most of the major helmet manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet every three to five years. This is due to things like sun exposure, normal use, and even repetitive small impacts over time. For riders looking for a higher level of performance out of a budget helmet, then consider the aero helmet from P2R. It’s priced at $100 and as our resident tester Tom Messina said, “it has no business being this good.”

I know, I know—a flat kit consists of multiple accessories. Typically my basic flat kit for people getting a new bike consists of: some type of inflation, tire levers, a multitool, the correct tube for the new bike, and something to carry it in. Some brands sell a flat pack that consists of all the above. If your new bike has internal storage and you plan on putting your flat kit in there, just be sure to make sure it all fits before your first ride.

Even for riders that have multiple bikes I suggest a new flat kit. Bikes have different requirements for tube sizes and valve types and lengths for different rims. There’s nothing worse than getting a flat and taking everything apart just to realize you have the wrong size tube or your valve isn’t long enough (let alone if your spare tube has a Schrader valve, but you need a presta).

If you have multiple bikes keeping a flat kit on each one also makes sense because when you’re taking a bike out you don’t have to switch around the flat kit. This means you’re less likely to forget something, and it takes away a hurdle from you getting out the door.

There are plenty of options to go with when considering inflation. I typically carry one to two CO2 cartridges and a CO2 inflator in a flat pack or frame storage because they take up such little room and can (sometimes) reset a bead on a tubeless tire. I also carry a frame-mounted hand pump on longer rides, because I’ve been stranded after running out of CO2 in the past. Mini electric inflators have been gaining steam in the past few years, and the convenience of them is hard to pass up.

A lot of bikes these days have more than one place to put a bottle cage, so if your new bike allows I suggest going with two bottle cages. Current full-suspension mountain bikes typically only fit one (I’m not a fan of a bottle on the down tube of a mountain bike), so that’s an exception to the suggestion.

I typically suggest recommending bottle cages to people getting a new bike over something like a hydration pack. The most impactful reason is because when you use a hydration pack it puts more weight on your sit bones when you ride. Water is one of the heaviest things you’ll carry on the bike, but you need it as you ride. Since you have to bring it, put that weight on the bike instead of having the weight sit on your sit bones.

There are two honorable mentions worth talking about—one has to do with safety and the other has to do with comfort. The first is a taillight. I didn’t mention it above because it’s less of a necessity if you’re strictly trail riding off road.

One of the things I would always hear about in the shop was, “but I’m not riding at night so I don’t need a tail light.” Daytime running lights have that name for a reason—you run them day or night. These lights help increase visibility of cyclists as we share the road with vehicles. Drivers can more easily spot riders thanks to varying strobe patterns of the light and some even have radar and cameras built in like the Garmin Varia series of lights. The radar in the Varia detects cars coming from behind and gives you a heads up on your phone, watch, or head unit. I couldn’t imagine riding on the road without a radar taillight at this point.

The second honorable mention is a pair of cycling shorts—specifically bike shorts that have a built-in chamois pad. These shorts help improve comfort like few other things when riding a bike. It took me years to convince my wife to try them, but now she won’t ride without a pair. I’ve tried a lot of bike shorts and I’ve learned that the bib style stay in place better throughout a ride compared to the standard shorts.

Another essential piece of advice when picking the right chamois is you get what you pay for. I’ve tried a $20 Amazon pair and I’m currently testing the Dottore Clima Bib Shorts from Q36.5. The Q36.5 bibs are by far the most comfortable bike shorts I have ever tried whether I’m doing shorter lunch rides or doing 100 mile gravel days. The flip side is they are also by far the most expensive pair of bike shorts I’ve ever tried, but there is a significant level of comfort no matter how many hours I’m in the saddle.

At this point it is safe to say that many of us have a smartphone. There are always exceptions, but throughout my time working in a shop I’ve come across a small handful of folks still using a flip phone. In addition to smartphones becoming an ingrained part of society, smartwatches are seen more and more on people’s wrists. If you have either of those things you don’t need a bike computer—especially to get into riding.

Bike computers are nice to have for training purposes and navigating a new area or route. But most of those things can be done on a phone or smart watch these days. I have used watches from Apple, COROS, and Garmin for tracking rides, navigation, and as a guide for training on a ride with success. If you’re a new rider and have a smartphone I typically suggest downloading Strava because it’s easy to track rides, the navigation tool is fairly user-friendly, and it’s easy to see your progress the more you ride.

Don’t get me wrong—I love my bike computer. It pools data from my heart-rate sensor, CORE body temperature sensor, cadence and power from my power meters, and even my sweat data through my Nix sensor. I can see every metric I can think of and most head units allow you to customize the layout on the screen. But the reality is that a worthwhile head unit is typically a few hundred dollars. Conversely the phone mount that I typically suggest costs less than $30 and is fairly universal. Bike computers make sense for some riders, but don’t start here if you’re prioritizing certain accessories over others for your new bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8948. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.

#8947. Bikepacking America's Longest Multiuse Trail Network

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Gas-station pizza, a medieval-themed hotel, canal and railroad bike path. Experience New York's multitudes on the Empire State Trail.

Even the slightest rain can sound thunderous inside a tent—and this was not slight rain. It came down in buckets, just as my partner Maggie and I were settling into our sleeping bags. I worried whether the barely-two-person tent would withstand a deluge like this and what the protocol was should lightning strike. And then lightning struck.

We talked about what to do. Maggie pulled up some information on her phone and was soon crouching on one foot, to avoid creating a circuit, she said with confidence. She counted the seconds between each flash and rumble out loud to gauge the storm’s proximity to us. I was mostly thinking of just how scant our escape options were. Our only way out was our drenched bicycles, resting against a soggy pine tree outside the tent. We took turns proposing different plans: spend the night in the campsite bathrooms, ride to the nearest motel, call the cops. We settled on hoping for the best. I fell asleep amid spiraling thoughts of dread: first night in, and this bike trip was already feeling like a mistake.

I woke up to the sound of birdsong and gentle raindrops, one beckoning me out of my sleeping bag, the other making a convincing argument to burrow deeper into it. But multiday bike touring, I would come to learn by the end of a 10-day journey across New York State’s Empire State Trail, is all about convincing yourself to do things you might not feel like doing—ride another dozen miles to the next town because it’s either that or a soulless highway motel, eat yet another granola bar because you didn’t plan lunch properly, wake up early to beat the hottest hours of the day—only to be thankful, eventually, that you did them.

Under a canopy of drizzle, Maggie and I emerged from our tent and went about a set of tasks that would soon become routine: We boiled water on our tiny camp stove for coffee and tea, broke down our sopping tent, repacked our panniers, and triple-checked that we left nothing behind. We were exhausted—a bad sign considering this was Day Two. But it was understandable, given how much we’d already experienced.

Starting in Buffalo, we’d decided to take a 65-mile pre-trip detour, cycling to Niagara Falls before looping back to start our real journey on the Empire State Trail that would take us all the way to New York City. We had already ridden through verdant farmland and industrial blight, had meandering conversations with strangers, and contended with the elements. A douchebag in a cheap sports car had almost run us off the road, but a bike shop mechanic at Campus WheelWorks in Buffalo had fixed my moody mechanical disc brakes on our way out of town and refused payment after he saw our panniers. We were the third bike tourers who had come through that week, he told us, but the first to have chosen to go west—to the falls—before heading east. He seemed to like that.

The morning after the storm, we caught our first glimpse of the Erie Canalway Trail, the western section of the Empire State Trail, which runs 360 miles from the shores of Lake Erie in Buffalo to the Hudson River in Albany. As far as we could see, we were the only people on this section. A finely ground gravel path, compacted by the rain, ran along the canal’s edge, straight and flat. A blanket of fog cloaked the waterway in an eerie silence. We stopped for a minute to take it in. Amid the quiet, I struggled to imagine the canal as the artery of industry it once had been. It was a long way yet to New York City.

On December 31, 2020, New York’s then-governor Andrew Cuomo announced the completion of the Empire State Trail, a 750-mile bike route, 75 percent of which is on car-free paths. The trail runs from Battery Park on the southern tip of Manhattan, up through the Hudson Valley and the Adirondacks to the border with Canada. Another section runs from Albany, all along the Erie Canal, to Buffalo. In all, it’s the largest multiuse trail network in the country.

While most sections existed before the establishment of the Empire State Trail, it took roughly four years—and about $200 million—to link them into a continuous network, a process that involved stakeholders ranging from individual municipalities to community volunteer groups, to the state’s parks department. “[The Empire State Trail is] easily 50 percent of my job now,” says Christopher Morris, the statewide trails program planner for New York State Parks, Recreation, and Historic Preservation. The trail isn’t overseen by a single entity; rather, it’s a kind of amorphous commonwealth of invested parties, each looking after their own section in favor of this greater mission. A major part of Morris’s job involves getting the word out, he says. He often gets emails from would-be travelers, from both the U.S. and abroad, looking for tips on how to navigate the trail. “When you really see this kind of investment make a difference, it’s rewarding,” he says. “It makes you feel good about your job.”

It’s understandable if you missed this bit of nerdy infrastructure news when the trail system opened. December 2020 was, up until that point, the deadliest month of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Over the preceding eight months, I’d holed away in a one-bedroom apartment in Manhattan, overwhelmed by a sense that the world I’d known and loved had ended. I’d spent the entirety of the previous year hopping week by week from destination to destination as The 52 Places Traveler for the New York Times, so the abrupt transition to total stasis left me feeling helpless—not to mention jobless. I welcomed the Empire State Trail news, which I heard about from hours of scrolling through Reddit looking for something—anything—to bring me out of my apartment and into the world again. Around four years earlier, I had splurged on a Trek CrossRip, a jack-of-all-trades, gravel-ish bike with an aluminum frame, after a lifetime of secondhand clunkers. Over time, I had made little upgrades—a Brooks saddle, handlebar tape that didn’t bleed dye onto my palms, bombproof Schwalbe tires to withstand New York City, where the streets are paved with glass. In the darkest days of the pandemic, that bike became my ticket out.

I rode whenever I could—through the empty streets of the city, the usual din of life being lived replaced by the constant wail of sirens; up and down the Hudson River Greenway on Manhattan’s West Side, itself part of the Empire State Trail. At around the same time I’d sprung for the Trek, Maggie had bought a Specialized Dolce, an aluminum all-rounder with rim brakes and what the company calls “Women’s Endurance Geometry.” She also fell in love with Brooks’s leather saddles and added in-line brake levers for extra safety. Together, we ventured farther afield. We followed the Empire State Trail up through the succession of rail trails in the Hudson Valley, veering off it to visit a friend in the Catskills. In the summer of 2021, I rented a car and drove my bike 275 miles up to Lake Champlain, where I explored the network’s most northerly sections through the Adirondacks, where the “trail” often is just a lane painted onto the side of a road—some of the 25 percent that isn’t car-free. I took locals’ advice to deviate from the main roads onto quieter country lanes, but I also found the rumble of logging trucks and tourist campervans whizzing by me oddly comforting, for it signaled a return to some kind of normalcy.

Spending so much time in transit for work has made home a moving target to me, often just out of reach and always out of focus. The bicycle, a tool invented to traverse distances efficiently, helped me see what was right in front of me.

In the early months of 2023, started to sketch out a trip I hoped would feel like a culmination of all my backyard wanderings around New York. Travel has always been a shortcut to adventure to me, and, because of that, I’ve often shorthanded adventure as requiring distance. I wondered if I could tap into the same thrills, all without ever stepping foot on a jet plane.

After a 10-hour train ride from New York City to Buffalo, I’d ride two main sections of the Empire State Trail—the west-to-east Erie Canal Trailway and the chain of rail trails and backroads running south from Albany back to my Harlem apartment—some 550 miles in all. Burdened by corporate vacation policies, Maggie decided she’d ride the Erie Canal section to Albany with me, then hop on the train home. In the months leading up to the trip, I pored over guides and online forums, of which there are many, building out a plan that involved a mix of camping and staying at bed-and-breakfasts in the towns along the way. Veterans of the trail warned of heavily trafficked sections of road around Kingston in the Hudson Valley and of the mosquitoes that swarmed the campsites at the various lock stations of the Erie Canal. Insiders cautioned against underestimating the coma-inducing qualities of a Rochester “garbage plate,” a bucketload of ground meat smothered in a fridge-tray’s worth of condiments. I took fastidious notes and drew up packing lists, weighing my panniers until I got to a weight I felt comfortable with. I plotted out days on the trail that would run us an average mileage of around 60, with a few “rest days” in the 30s baked in.

Seasoned bikepackers and bike tourers may find this all a little overdramatic. But having really only fallen hard for cycling in the last few years, I still don’t understand many things: a bike’s head-tube angle and trail; heart-rate zones and watts. But I do know travel. I know that so many of the clichés are true: that the best travel moments often appear out of the haze of the unexpected; that the journey can mean much more than the destination; that risk almost always reaps rewards; that who you travel with is often more important than where you go; that everywhere, no matter how seemingly mundane or obscure, has a little bit of magic waiting to reveal itself, if you just let it.

When it opened in 1825, the Erie Canal was the longest artificial waterway in North America and, in how it opened up the interior of the country to enterprising East Coasters, it was an embodiment of a pioneer mindset that saw a burgeoning country shape the land to its will and expand farther west. While it wouldn’t take long for the railway to replace canal barges as the go-to freight hauler, the political will and sheer toil that went into the canal’s construction would be a precursor to the hyper-capitalist nation emerging in the following centuries. “In time, this skinny ditch in upstate New York would demonstrate that trade and commerce are keys to the expansion of prosperity and freedom itself,” writes the historian Peter L. Bernstein in his 2005 history of the canal, The Wedding of the Waters.

Many of the settlements along the canal aren’t thriving like they were when this was a major thoroughfare of trade. Once tracing a path between vibrant industrial hubs, the waterway now closely mirrors the contours of the Rust Belt. Just as the grandeur of Victorian mansions points to what was, so do empty streets and faded “For Rent” signs on empty storefronts.

One such town, Brockport, is at least partially buoyed by the state university campus—or so I was told by Valerie Ciciotti, who runs Park Ave B&B in a painstakingly restored 1851 mansion that we stayed in. Graduation is the busiest time, she says, but bike tourists like us are becoming more common every summer. As we rolled out of Brockport the next morning, I wondered—not for the last time—whether a steady influx of tired, hungry cyclists could be enough to keep towns along the canal alive. (When I caught up with Ciciotti recently, she said the trail was already making a difference—the village government has become more directly involved with tourism, including designating Brockport an official Empire State Trail Town.)

We spent the next week on the Erie Canal in a kind of meditative rhythm that only comes from long trips, drifting in and out of conversations with each other, keeping count of kingfishers flitting along the water, and gasping when a heron swallowed a fish whole.

Outside Fairport, the skies turned black and dumped rain on us until we were laughing at the absurdity of trying to cycle through mud so dense it made our tires seize. Bystanders, wise enough to take shelter, cheered us on as we rode. We stopped under an awning and pried mud from our chains with our fingers. When the rain showed no sign of stopping, we just kept going—pulled along by the promise of a hot shower and a cold beer. We rode through sheets of rain until water poured out of our shoes. Once the deluge slowed, we tied wet clothes to our bikes. We looked like sailboats rolling down the trail.

One night, we camped at one of the locks along the trail, where boats are lifted to account for elevation changes in the ground. (Cyclists can camp at certain locks for free but are encouraged to call the lockkeeper ahead of time as a courtesy.) As the light faded and the mosquitoes emerged, I spoke to a pair of retirees on a boat who were following the same path as so many goods-bearing barges once did—from the Great Lakes to the Hudson and the sea. We woke up in the middle of the night to the infernal shrieks of nearby foxes. The following morning, we rode into Utica for breakfast at Golden’s diner, itself a throwback, where one man behind a counter flipped eggs and pointed to the self-service coffee station while bebop played from tinny speakers.

For our last night on the canal, we stayed in the Amsterdam Castle, which looms over the tiny town of Amsterdam like a tyrant’s keep. A bizarre manifestation of some sort of Arthurian fantasy, the hotel features suits of armor in the lobby and velvet bedding in the rooms. New York State truly contains multitudes.

I thought about all the many things I’d seen and done in my travels to far-flung places—witnessing a solar eclipse in Chile, kayaking alongside humpbacks in Antarctica, hiking through prehistoric rainforests in New Zealand. If novelty is what drives our travel decisions, it was rapidly becoming clear to me that I didn’t always need to fling myself halfway around the world to find it.

Because the Empire State Trail is mostly a consolidation of existing paths and an effort to fill the gaps between them—and because of the vast distances the network covers—the character of the trail changes the farther along it you ride. I noticed this as soon as I said goodbye to Maggie in Albany at the eastern terminus of the Erie Canal and turned south on the first of a number of rail trails that would take me back to New York City over the next three days. With the canal no longer a constant companion, I found myself instead passing through bucolic suburbs, open farmland, and, occasionally, dense sections of forest. Riding alone after days with someone else was an adjustment, too. I found, just a few hours after turning south, I was talking to myself—making observations about the lack of shade and the odd, ashy taste in my mouth from forest fire smoke drifting south from Canada. It made for tough riding—and I took much more frequent rest stops.

When planning my trip, I knew I’d pass through major regional hubs like Hudson and Kingston. But I also wanted to experience corners of the state I hadn’t seen before, and I chose my stops for the night with that in mind. That’s how I ended up veering a mile off the trail into the storybook village of Kinderhook. I checked into the luxurious Old Dutch Inn, a new hotel housed in a modernized 19th-century building with views of the village square. It had only just opened a few weeks prior. The co-owner, Jennifer Ose-MacDonald, showed no trepidation when she welcomed my mud-streaked, sweat-drenched self into her immaculate establishment, where snow-white linens hung from the windows. Knowing I was one of the first of what she hoped to be many bike-traveler guests, she asked me for advice on bike racks. I told her that though the exact model of bike rack wasn’t that important, alas, a lot of cyclists might not be as comfortable locking up their bikes outside overnight as I was. (Ose-MacDonald says she has since carved out space for indoor bike storage and has added a trove of tools for cycling guests.)

Ose-Macdonald’s partner, Jake Samascott, runs a much-visited orchard and farm shop in town but is also the president of the Columbia Friends of the Electric Trail, an organization of volunteers who maintain the section of trail that passes through Columbia County, mowing and trimming the greenery around the path. For years it was an unused, overgrown corridor through which power lines ran. More than a thoroughfare for bike tourists like me, the trail is a community asset, Samascott says. “I have three little girls who wanted to learn to ride bikes—I want them riding on a trail and not on the road.”

I saw how these paths build community throughout my trip but especially on the rail trails that run one into another through the Hudson Valley until they end in Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx. Travelers like me were few and far between, but I passed dozens of families out on bikes, joggers with their dogs, even summer-school groups. Several, seeing my bags, and the level of grime on my face and body, would offer a thumbs-up or shout, “You’re almost there,” though they didn’t know where I was going.

New York State isn’t all smooth-rolling. Idyllic sections of tree-shaded gravel paths on rail trails are broken up by hilly roads and, at one point around Kingston, a traffic-snarled bridge. Unlike the Erie Canal section, campsites along the Albany-NYC axis of the trail are largely nonexistent, which means budgeting for hotels, and that can be pricey, especially during the summer high season. The penultimate stretch of trail, leading to the town of Brewster, inches steadily uphill for at least 15 miles, which, after more than a week of long days, felt like I was conquering the Dolomites. Arriving in Brewster—still about 50 miles from the northern edge of New York City—I found none of the charming, independent B&Bs or idyllic campsites I had depended so much on during my trip. I could have opted to make a break for it and ride a century straight from the Poughkeepsie area to the city on my last day, but I didn’t have it in me. I bought a gas-station beer the size of my head, checked into a soulless Comfort Inn, and ordered a pizza.

Over the course of the whole trip, 11 days in all, I thought often about infrastructure and movement; about how much effort has gone into inventing new ways to travel, ever faster, ever cheaper, ever more efficient. By the time the Erie Canal was completed, the railroad was already ascendant. On large sections of the Hudson Valley’s various rail trails, the rusted remains of iron rails sit, fossilized and inert. Alongside them, on the very beds of dirt where they once ran, the gravel is crisscrossed with bike-tire tracks and packed down with the footprints of millions of pedestrians.

I stopped often, to stretch, to photograph, to think. As it does when traveling on your own power, every mile felt like an achievement, no matter how repetitive and, at moments, no matter how difficult the actions were. Even while choking on smoke, with my legs burning and my bike making new and unfamiliar sounds (brake rub, it turned out), I found myself drawn onward by a sense of discovery—the feeling that I was getting a more solid picture of a concept that has eluded me for most of my life: home.

The closer I got to New York City, the more anything resembling silence was replaced with the constant whir of nearby interstates. Planes rumbled overhead. How much faster can we possibly go? What comes next in our constant hunt for peak efficiency? And what will we do with all that extra free time, anyway? The bike and all the places it can take me beckon.

Sebastian Modak is a writer, editor, and photographer based in New York City. He spent 2019 circling the globe as the New York Times 52 Places Traveler, reporting from every destination on the Times’ 52 Places to Go list.
