#8932. Stop Cramming Bikes in Your Car. These 10 Editor-Tested Hitch Racks Make Hauling Easier and More Secure

Our editors hauled bikes for thousands of miles to find the easiest, sturdiest hitch racks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cramming your bike into your car or SUV gets old quickly. Removing wheels and getting mud or grease all over your interior is no fun, and transporting your bike inside your car also leaves less room for passengers, luggage, or gear. Hitch-mount racks are the easiest, most secure way to carry your bike to your riding destination without mess or hassle. They’re ideal for heading to your local mountain bike trails, taking a road trip with friends, or going for weekend rides with your kids.

Hitch racks mount to the receiver on your vehicle’s bumper, making hitch racks easier to load than roof racks—hoisting a heavy bike onto an SUV’s roof after a long ride is never fun. Plus, you don’t need to remove your front wheel. Unlike roof racks, you can also drive into parking garages and drive-thrus with bikes on a hitch rack. And importantly, in an era of sky-high fuel prices, hitch racks typically impact your gas mileage less than roof-mounted options.

While hitch racks usually cost more than simple, low-cost trunk-mount racks, they can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. Hitch-mount carriers can also carry heavier bikes, like electric bikes or full suspension rigs, than trunk racks and are more stable at highway speeds.

Our editors and test team evaluated dozens of hitch racks to see which ones perform best. Our staff has used some of these racks on their own vehicles for years, safely transporting bikes over tens of thousands of miles. Our picks for the best hitch-mounted bike racks vary in features like position, trunk access functionality, bike capacity, and price—but all are dependable options for your next cycling trip.

Based on price, weight capacity, and ease of use, Thule’s Outpace ranks as our current Best Overall pick. The Outpace is lighter and more compact than most hitch racks, which makes it easy to install and remove. At only 28 pounds, it’s light enough to carry across the garage and slide into the receiver tube. Setup takes less than a minute, so you can mount it on the car when you need to haul your bikes (rather than it semi-permanently living on your bumper).

The rack can accommodate a wider range of bike wheel sizes, making it great for families. The rack adapts easily to any size bicycle in either position. The tradeoff for this versatility is that it takes a bit longer to load than bulkier racks with cinch-style clamps. But for something that can carry all of our bikes, and is so quick to install or remove that it never has to be a permanent fixture, that’s a small price to pay.

Our tester noted the Outpace’s receiver arm is on the short side. It fit snugly against the bumper with about two inches to spare, but on another vehicle, it wouldn’t fit without a hitch extender.

The Trail Rider is a great, lower-cost alternative to premium racks. It holds two bikes in fixed wheel mounts, secured with a single ratcheting arm that clamps down over the frame. The upright beam (which holds the frame holders) folds back and out of the way for trunk access; it’s also handy for loading up two bikes. We could fold it down, set a bike on the rack closest to the car without lifting it up and over the arm, then lift the arm back into place and position the second bike.

The trade-off for the Trail Rider’s low price isn’t stability or strength, but adjustability: The bikes are positioned in a fixed location. You have limited ability to separate them if two bikes don’t fit well together. That said, you can stagger the wheel cradles so the bars and saddles don’t interfere.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected at this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Lastly, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

The Piston Pro X is our runner-up for Best Overall hitch rack; its construction, features, and style make it a standout pick in the category. Aside from the high price, the Piston Pro X is almost the perfect hitch rack for most users.

With the Piston Pro X, Küat elevated the rack from something purely utilitarian to a desirable piece of gear that’s easier to use than other racks. The rack includes smart features (such as integrated brake and turn-signal lights) and can carry more wheel sizes (and more weight) than almost any other rack on the market.

The top-end Pro X model costs more than almost any other hitch-mount rack, but it has proven extremely durable and maintains its good looks. It's also available in 3- and 4-bike models. Küat also offers a slightly cheaper Piston Pro variant, which ditches the Kashima coating on the pistons and the integrated brake lights and turn signals.

If you like the Küat racks but $1,600 is out of your price range, the brand offers several other hitch-style racks that could meet your needs. One great option is the Sherpa 2.0 model.

While the Sherpa doesn’t have the features or carrying capacity of Küat’s more expensive racks, it has two big upsides—color options and low weight. The Sherpa weighs only 32 pounds (claimed) in the 2-inch hitch configuration (1.25-in. also available). Küat offers the Sherpa in three colors: black metallic (with a silver accent), grey metallic (with orange), and pearl white (with silver).

The Sherpa carries two bicycles weighing up to 40 pounds per tray. So it’s ideal for non-electric road, gravel, and mountain bikes. It has an integrated cable lock to secure your bikes during rest stops or meal breaks, and it features a foot-operated lever to lower the rack into position for loading bikes.

It’s often difficult to carry e-bikes that are equipped with racks and fenders on traditional hitch racks. That’s because many hitch racks secure the bike with extending arms that clamp one or both wheels. However, Thule’s EasyFold XT model holds your bike by its frame.

Another feature that makes the EasyFold ideal for e-bike owners is the included ramp. This makes loading or removing your bikes much easier; no more wrestling with heavy bikes or front wheels or handlebars flopping as you load them onto the rack. And the ramp attaches to the rack when you’re finished.

Thanks to the rack’s 45-pound weight, it’s easy to remove it from your vehicle when you’re not using it. It folds down and features casters (which make moving it around your garage easier). The EasyFold XT’s biggest drawback is that Thule only rates it to 65 pounds per bike. While that will accommodate many e-bikes, some fat tire models may weigh too much.

When Thule debuted the T2 over a decade ago, it raised the bar for what cyclists expect from a hitch-mounted bike rack. Over the years, Thule updated the rack to accommodate wider tires and different wheel sizes. It also improved the T2’s look and made it easier to operate. One of the best recent upgrades is a wide-trigger handle that allows you to raise and lower the rack (and dip it out of the way for access to rear hatches) with one hand.

Integrated cable locks help keep your bikes secure for quick stops, and each tray can hold a bicycle up to 60 pounds and tires up to 5 inches wide. This makes the T2 a good option for all but the heaviest e-bikes. The T2 Pro’s arms have wide, comfortable grips that slide easily to secure the front wheel. Instead of using a bolt, the rack secures to your hitch receiver with an expansion wedge that tightens with a locking knob. The system makes installing and removing the T2 easier (though it weighs 52 pounds), but it’s not foolproof.

Yakima’s StageTwo two-bike rack goes head-to-head with premium offerings from Küat and Thule at a lower price. In about 2,500 miles of on-car testing, the StageTwo impressed us with its ease of use and flex-free performance. This rack is only rated up to 35 pounds per tray, so it’s not made for transporting e-bikes. However, it’s one of only two racks on this list that accommodates wheels as small as 16 inches.

The StageTwo’s trays are offset, which means less chance of contact when carrying two similarly sized bikes (however, bikes sit more widely apart, so watch those tight parking spaces). The rack includes two SKS locking cables (they don’t auto-retract, so tuck them back in when not in use). The StageTwo also includes an integrated lock loop for extra security when parked or locking your rack off the vehicle.

The rack is offered in 1.25- and 2-inch sizes. The 2-inch variant can accommodate four bikes with an add-on kit. Also, check Yakima’s fit guide before buying—One of our testers experienced a hardware fitment issue.

If you travel to mountain resort towns (or have been around trailheads or bike parks lately), you’ve probably seen behemoth racks like these on the back of vans and trucks. Since modern mountain bikes are bulky, racks like Thule’s ReVert make sense if you’re hauling a full load with a single vehicle.

The ReVert holds six bikes, loads quickly, and sticks out no farther than a standard 2-bike horizontal rack. Its carrying capacity makes it ideal for large families, race teams, or ride groups.

At over 87 pounds, the ReVert is undeniably heavy. However, a few smart features make the rack manageable. Dual hydraulic dampers assist with lowering the rack when it’s fully loaded, so you don’t have to wrestle with it. Once in the lowered position, even shorter riders and kids can lift their bikes high enough to slot them into the baskets. Individual bikes are spaced 11 inches apart, giving you plenty of room to carry any combination—flat bar, drop bar, even cruisers.

1UP USA has built a cult-like following with its industrial-looking racks that take a simplistic approach to securing your bike. This model features two ratcheting arms that clamp down on your wheels—no hooks or straps necessary.

The Equip-D’s pivot mechanism is smooth and reliable even after years of abuse (although an occasional shot of WD-40 White Lithium Grease Spray goes a long way in keeping the release mechanism running smoothly). A T-handle release positioned at the end of the hitch bar means you don’t need to reach through the rack to fold it up. Tiered trays position bikes closer together, and the rack rides out of the way of most exhaust pipes. 1Up also offers the Equip in a single-bike version for a sleeker look.

Hitch racks are bicycle carriers that attach to your vehicle’s hitch receiver. Popular models carry one to four bikes, but some hanging-style hitch racks can haul up to six bikes.

A hitch is a standard feature on most trucks and many SUVs. However, if you have a car or wagon, a hitch can often be added. If your vehicle doesn’t already have a receiver, it’s easy to have one installed. (U-Haul is a reliable and affordable option for installation.)Receivers come in two sizes: 1¼-inch and 2-inch (measured across the inside of the square opening). Most trucks and SUVs use a 2-inch receiver. Many racks are available in both sizes, but heavier-duty racks—and racks that carry three or more bikes—often require the larger 2-inch receiver for added strength and stability. Racks rated to carry heavyweight e-bikes also typically require a 2-inch receiver.

If the rack will live on your vehicle year-round or see frequent use, invest in the most durable model your budget allows. While all racks listed here secure bikes effectively, higher-priced options tend to have sturdier moving parts—ratchets, straps, buckles, and locks—that stand up better to long-term use.

Not all hitch racks are rated for the extra weight of e-bikes. Those that aren’t suited for heavier bikes are clearly noted in our reviews.

Some racks are quite heavy, which contributes to their strength but can be inconvenient if you plan to remove and reinstall the rack frequently.

For most vehicles—aside from sedans—accessing the trunk or tailgate is restricted when the rack is in use or folded up. Many of our top picks offer tilt-down designs that allow you to open the back of your vehicle even with bikes loaded. For full access, swing-away adapters like the Küat Pivot v2 Swing-Away allow the entire rack to pivot 90 degrees, completely clearing the rear of your car or truck.

Need more clearance? Sometimes a simple hitch extender can do the trick. For added stability and peace of mind, we also recommend using an anti-rattle clamp with any rack you choose.

Pros: Hitch racks strike the perfect balance between the ease of access of a trunk rack and the security of a quality roof rack. They slot into your car’s hitch receiver, relying on no flimsy straps or sketchy hooks. They’re also positioned behind your car, which is great for gas mileage and roof-collision prevention (low standing height). Better yet, many are modular, allowing you to add extra trays, locks, and even bottle openers for more personalized functionality.

Cons: These racks are the most consistently expensive out there—quality materials and a confidence-inspiring construction unquestionably affect their price. Furthermore, they can be a pain to remove, as most options weigh well over 40 pounds and need tools to detach. Furthermore, with bikes on the rack, they add significant length to your vehicle, which could prove tricky if you need to parallel park. And most critically, not every car has a hitch, which means you’ll either need to install one yourself or forego this style entirely.

Our editors drove hundreds (and in some cases, thousands) of miles with their bikes on these racks. We hauled road bikes, mountain bikes, e-bikes, and city bikes. We carried bikes with disc brakes, big wheels, and fat tires. Our test team used these racks for months, in various environments and conditions. We tested them in the salty winters of Pennsylvania, the high mountains of Colorado, and the gritty Arizona desert.

These racks in this story stand out for their ease of installation and use, lack of play in key areas, manageable weight, and bike capacity. We also looked for sharp prices and deals.

Whether you’re a roadie on the way to your next fondo, a mountain biker heading to the trailhead, or loading up the family for a weekend adventure, our rack picks will cover whatever needs you and your riding crew may have.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8931. Julius Thomas Speaks His Mind When It Comes to Peak Performance

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

When Julius Thomas hung up his NFL cleats in 2018, he didn’t know he was about to face the hardest, and longest, transition of his life. The tight end who caught touchdowns from Peyton Manning walked into graduate school at 30 with no job, no playbook, and none of the daily wins football used to hand him.

“When you have to go from a master to a rookie, you go from winning a lot, knowing what you’re doing and very comfortable with all of it, to then having to rebuild that,” he recalled. “That is extremely challenging, because in the beginning of any journey, it’s losing, doing it wrong, working really hard, struggling through it.”

The lessons he learned over the years that followed changed the way he looked at performance. He went back to the classroom, completed a clinical residency and earned his doctorate in clinical psychology in June 2025.

In pro sports, the mentality is often to push through and keep going. While Thomas lived that for years, today, as a performance coach and consultant with his company Optimal Performance, he sees how much of peak performance relies on stepping back and checking in with ourselves.

“One of the things I say is the biggest unaddressed area of performance in all of sport is emotional regulation,” Thomas told Muscle & Fitness.

The 2026 NFL season has already tested the push-through mindset from the opening weeks. Six of the 32 quarterbacks initially named starters were hurt early in the season, including Jayden Daniels, Caleb Williams and Jaxson Dart. Now Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is now expected to miss the rest of the season after doctors found deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, with his case traced back to a calf injury from an opponent’s cleat.

Thomas resisted pinning the run on any single cause. He also didn’t think any of this was unusual. “Football has a 100% injury rate” he says. “Every single person that plays football is going to get injured, so injuries are just high in that sport in general.”

Contact injuries come with the job, he said, while training loads, surfaces, off-season habits, mobility, and recovery—or the lack thereof—shape the non-contact ones. Research has also shown that the mind does have a seat at the table.

A 2017 meta-analysis in Sports Medicine linked stress responses to higher injury risk and found psychological interventions reduced injury rates. Hence, Thomas makes it a point to take our foot off the gas a lot more frequently than we do.

“If you just only floor it, only floor it, only floor it. How long do you think that engine is going to do well?” Thomas explains. “Not very long.”

The brakes represent the parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-and-digest branch that counters the stress response. “If we don’t do enough to create more parasympathetic tone in our nervous system, if we don’t sleep enough hours, all we’re doing is degrading the major systems in our body,” he explained, noting the cost of the grind will come sooner or later.

This pattern follows high performers into the boardroom as well. Thomas has coached executives who asked him for nootropics to sharpen their focus—then admitted that he himself was only getting four hours of sleep a night for 20 years. So he’s built a framework called “Striving for 100” to bring clients back to five daily habits, including exercise, sleep, nutrition, recovery and healthy substance use, with recovery anchoring the rest. One-on-one, he layers in radical acceptance, cognitive restructuring and reframing drawn from several evidence-based methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).

“You’re either gonna pay the cost slowly and surely by recovering in your 30s and 40s and 50s,” he says, “or you’re gonna pay it all of a sudden when you’re sick.”

He holds himself to the same standard. Though when a friend had warned him a full transition would take about a decade, he refused to believe it.

“I am eight years in transition. And I’m almost to where I want to be in my next profession,” he admitted, but pointed out the difficulty he’s experienced with identity and how much our society gets it wrong.

Thomas bristles at the advice athletes often hear on the way out, that they simply need to separate who they are from the sport they played.

“It really bothers me when people say that about athletes, because they’re trying to minimize the challenge of the experience, so that when the athlete finds himself in the psychological challenge, they feel like they shouldn’t be, and this should be easy,” he explained, adding that identity runs deeper than a label, and it’s built by what you do every day and reinforced by how others see you.

Years after his last game, people still want to talk about NFL playing days, in which the two-time Pro Bowl tight end caught 12 touchdown passes in both 2012 and 2013. “It’s hard to get people to see you in your new career,” he admitted.

Now he prepares athletes for that shift and asks them whether they’re ready for one of the hardest things they’ll ever do, and whether they’ve built the tools to get through it.

“Do you have the psychological skills to reframe, recontextualize, find meaning, find purpose?” he’d ask.

What he doesn’t want any player to forget is that the struggle says nothing about them. Every major life change strains us. “Transitions are always hard,” he said. But with the right tools and support, it becomes easier to navigate over time.

Most of us were never taught to name what we feel, let alone work through it when stress drags on for months. Thomas wasn’t either, and he’s seen the toll it could take on the body.

“Emotions trigger our nervous system,” he says, referring to his studies in psychoneuroimmunology. “So the better you get at managing emotions and reducing negative emotions, the less sustained stress you’d have on your nervous system.”

And it matters because our nervous system, immune system, and psychology are connected, he says, and when stress becomes chronic, various aspects of our life take a hit. Sleep and diet slip first when emotional strain builds, he noted, and muscle tension climbs as anxiety lingers.

However, simply putting a feeling into words can help turn the volume down. A 2007 UCLA brain imaging study in Psychological Science found that labeling emotions dampened the amygdala’s response to negative images.

Though few of us get support doing that work. He cited CDC data that reported 10.9% of U.S. men receive counseling or therapy from a mental health professional, compared with 16.9% of women. And, unfortunately, Thomas sees where we choose to spend time and money instead.

“People are not interested in paying for mental health services, but they’re really interested in new pants and new shirts and nice bags,” he said, adding how much easier it is for many of us to ask for help with physical pain or discomfort. As a player, he never hesitated to walk into the training room with a sore ankle.

“We are constantly asking for help in so many areas of our life,” he says, “but we somehow, as a culture, believe that we should handle what’s in our heart and in our mind by ourselves.”

Certainly, Thomas is no rookie in his new career, and it shows in the company he keeps. At Eudēmonia on November 5-8, he will share the stage with some of the movers and shakers of the health, wellness and longevity industry.

He recalled his first year at the event and how much the relationships he built across psychology, neuroscience, medicine and mind-body practices have stayed with him.

“The conversations, the network, the community I built at year one at Eudēmonia is still having positive influence on my life almost one year later,” he said. “And Eudēmonia has become one of the conferences that I’m most excited to go to.”

Thomas returns with keynotes on mental health and a panel discussion on mindset, performance and the capacity to adapt. The takeaway he wants the audience to leave with is hope, actionable steps, and to be educated in something that is going to help make them healthier, better, more productive and higher functioning.

“If you want sustainable high performance, you have to build well-being and quality of life into what you do,” he said.

#8930. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8929. Here’s How A Cruel Ironman Finish Turned Into Kona Gold Redemption

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The last mile of an Ironman is a terrible place to discover that your body has filed for bankruptcy. You’ve already swum 2.4 miles, ridden a bicycle 112, and run far enough to qualify as a perfectly respectable marathon. All that’s left is a little strip of asphalt and a finish line. Unfortunately, at that point, your legs don’t give a shit about your plans, your sponsors, or the fact that the whole world is watching.

On October 10, the Ironman World Championship in Kona, HI, produced the kind of finish that makes a Hollywood sports movie look underwritten. American Taylor Knibb won the women’s race in 8:36:29. Defending champion Solveig Løvseth, who had taken the lead from her with about five miles to go, began to stagger in the final mile, stopped, and went down. Knibb came past and took the title. Løvseth eventually got up, continued, and finished eighth. Germany’s Laura Philipp was second, Switzerland’s Julie Derron third.

Now for the part that makes this story extraordinary. A year earlier, the same two women were in essentially the opposite positions. Knibb had been leading the 2025 race when she broke down late in the marathon, and Løvseth went by her to win. Knibb didn’t finish. So, twelve months later, the woman who suffered the heartbreak became the champion, and the woman who benefited from it suffered the heartbreak. If you wrote that into a screenplay, some producer would tell you it was too obvious.

There’s a temptation to turn this into one of those inspirational posters about never quitting. Resist it. Neither woman lacked determination. Knibb had already won the 2026 Ironman 70.3 World Championship, which is only a half Ironman if your definition of half includes several hours of punishment. Løvseth was defending the biggest title in the sport. Both were capable of winning. The deciding factor wasn’t who wanted it more. It was who could still function when the clock had been running for eight and a half hours.

And before the internet’s medical experts announce exactly what happened to Løvseth, we don’t have a confirmed diagnosis that establishes the cause of her collapse. Heat, hydration, fueling, and accumulated exertion are obvious things to examine in an event like Kona. But looking at somebody wobbling on a road and diagnosing an electrolyte deficiency from your couch isn’t sports medicine. Collapse during exertion can signal a medical emergency and warrants medical assessment. Determination is admirable, but turning a potential medical emergency into a motivational slogan is stupid.

The men’s race had its own little piece of lunacy. Vincent Luis of France, 37 years old and making his Kona world championship debut, won in 7:47:27. This wasn’t some anonymous guy who stumbled out of a cycling club. Luis had already competed in the Olympics and won world titles at shorter triathlon distances. He had also talked about retiring. Instead, he went to Hawaii, passed Denmark’s Magnus Ditlev during the marathon, and beat former champion Gustav Iden by about a minute and a half. American Matthew Marquardt took third.

For the first time since 2019, the men’s and women’s professional championships were held together in Kona. Both races delivered late reversals, which tells you something about the difference between being the strongest athlete on paper and being the strongest athlete at the finish. You can train for the distance, practice your nutrition, dial in your equipment, and prepare for the heat. You absolutely should. But there isn’t a training program on earth that guarantees your body will cooperate for 140.6 miles.

I’m not suggesting everybody needs to do an Ironman. Personally, I can think of several hundred more pleasant ways to spend a Saturday. But anybody who has ever trained seriously recognizes the lesson. The race isn’t over because you’re ahead. It isn’t over because you’re behind. And occasionally, the biggest victory isn’t crossing first. It’s recognizing when the race has taken enough out of you. The last mile has no respect for reputation, and it sure as hell doesn’t care who was winning at mile 139.

#8925. That Mysterious Bike Creak Is Driving You Crazy—Here’s How to Check Your Bottom Bracket

Simple checks to pinpoint bottom bracket creaks before they become bigger repairs.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves, or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. When I ran a shop, we would have customers come in and they would be certain that a noise was coming from one spot—only to find the culprit be somewhere else. Many times a noise would originate at the cranks or bottom bracket, so that’s what we’ll focus on here.

It’s worth checking on the lowest hanging fruit before we dig into the bottom bracket. The most common noisemakers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM DUB and Race Face Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

It’s also possible you simply need a new bottom bracket in the bike. Bottom bracket standards are a deep rabbit hole and can feel overly complex if you aren’t familiar with the system. Different frames and different cranks require different bottom brackets. Before searching Amazon for the best deal on bottom brackets, consult the technical specifications for your specific bike and component group or visit your local shop for direction.

I have seen bottom bracket issues actually cause issues on carbon frames as well. I’ve seen this specifically on older carbon frames with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained over time. All the bikes that I saw frame issues from bottom brackets fell into the same category: older carbon road bikes with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained for years. Eventually the customer would hear a noise, but keep riding. Then that noise would turn into knocking in the crank. By the time they got to our shop, the space in the frame for the bottom bracket was no longer a perfect circle. That circle shifted into an oval over time—which more times than not resulted in a new frame being needed. If you have a creak in your bottom bracket, get it checked out (or inspect it yourself) before it becomes something bigger.

#8924. Zipp’s Cheapest Carbon Wheelset Makes a Strong Case for Itself—But There’s One Catch

A major-brand carbon wheelset at a lower price, with a great warranty and one trade-off road riders should consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Zipp’s 404S replaces the 303S with a deeper 50mm rim for modern road riding. Zipp says the new profile saves about two watts over its predecessor. At $1,300 for the pair, the wheels bring a familiar name and a lifetime warranty to a price well below the brand’s flagship models.

I rode the 404S on my steel Ritchey Road Logic, logging roughly 800 miles over two months. They’re a totally fine, solid wheelset. They feel settled at speed without riding harshly, accelerate well once they’re rolling, and remain stable in gusty conditions. In other words, Zipp made a perfectly good wheelset that will likely come stock on many SRAM-equipped bikes.

On the road, the 404S fades into the background of your ride (in a good way). The wheels feel comfortable without feeling harsh. Get them up to speed, and they are reassuringly solid. In terms of crosswind performance, I’d rate them quite good. They aren’t quite on the level of something like a Roval Rapide CLX III (basically the gold standard for crosswind performance), but they still feel very stable even on a gusty day. Once I'm moving, they have the responsive feel I expect from a 50mm wheelset, whether I’m pedaling through a corner or getting back up to speed on a rolling road.

The weight shows up more on steep climbs or when accelerating out of a slow corner; these wheels don’t have the immediate, lively feel of lighter aero options. That doesn’t make them feel sluggish in normal riding; it’s just the clearest difference I noticed after riding lighter wheels.

Otherwise, I found little to separate the 404S from more expensive wheelsets with a similar rim depth. They do the basic job well: they feel stable in the wind, comfortable on imperfect roads, and once you’re up to speed, their weight disadvantage largely disappears.

The 404S uses a Tubeless Straight Side, or hookless, rim design. That means checking tire compatibility and pressure limits before you ride. Zipp recommends tires from 28 to 39mm, and says the wheels are optimized for 28–29mm tires for best aero performance, with a maximum pressure of 72.5 psi. Many riders might miss that if you run a 30 or 32mm road tire, the maximum pressure limit drops to 65 psi, according to ETRTO.

Those limits may not affect riders who already use wider tires at lower pressures. But I still see hookless as a miss for road wheels in 2026 for many reasons. Sure, a handful of high-profile issues in the pro peloton didn’t help, but neither did the steady drip of unease coming from inside the industry itself. While Zipp has stood behind the standard, I’d rather give the company credit for acknowledging that many riders (including me) would prefer a hooked option. instead of dealing with a relatively low max tire-pressure limit, consulting pressure charts, and reading tire-compatibility lists.

ENVE, arguably the biggest proponent of hookless road wheels, has already made this pivot. The brand's flagship racing models, the SES 4.5 and 6.7 Pro wheels, both feature a “mini hook.” This leaves only Zipp and Giant/Cadex sticking with hookless for now, and given my predictions earlier this year, I would guess both are at least considering their options.

At $1,300, the 404S sits between a few other 50mm carbon wheelsets. HUNT’s 50 Carbon Disc is listed at $1,249, with a 50mm rim, 22mm internal width, and a hooked tire interface. HUNT lists its weight at 1,464 grams, making it a close alternative for about $50 less, with a hooked rim.

Shimano’s Ultegra C50 is another 50mm option, listed at $1,570 for the pair. It has a hooked rim and a 21mm internal width, making it a little more expensive than the Zipp, with a narrower rim bed.

The harder comparison for Zipp is basically any wheel from Light Bicycle. Light Bicycle’s complete Airia wheel builds start at $1,144, and that base build is claimed to weigh 1,218 grams. The 55mm-deep test set weighed 1,101 grams without tape or valves, though that specific build cost about $1,407. So the tested Airias were slightly more expensive than the 404S, but they were 5mm deeper and dramatically lighter (also hooked).

That makes the 404S a reasonably priced option from a major brand, but the weight is hard to overlook when lighter and sometimes cheaper wheels are available at similar or lower prices. But the 404S does have one way it stands above its competition. It comes with a lifetime warranty that covers not just manufacturing defects but also damage from intended use. This will appeal to many riders who would rather have a dependable wheel than a slightly lighter one.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:

All transfers are instant. This matters because ANA business class availability on partner programs is scarce, and when you find a seat, you need to move fast. You cannot afford to wait 3–5 days for points to post.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

With miles now in your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, complete the booking at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com. Use the flight numbers you identified in Step 2. You should see $0 in fuel surcharges — only government taxes (typically $50–$100 for trans-Pacific routing).

Airlines partner with each other through alliances and bilateral agreements, allowing their frequent flyer programs to book seats on each other's flights. The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan. You've been dreaming about it for years — Tokyo, Kyoto, the food, the culture. You want to arrive rested and ready, not wrecked from 14 hours in economy.

Two passengers, one-way: 180,000 Virgin Atlantic miles. That's not an abstraction — that's a real number that changes the calculus of what's possible on a FI timeline.

ANA releases partner award space 331 days in advance. For a popular route like JFK–NRT, the best business class availability — especially on "The Room" 777-300ER services — can disappear within days of release. Mark your calendar. Search at exactly 331 days out for your target travel dates.

Transfers are instant from all major partners, which is powerful — but it also means there's no excuse for transferring before you have confirmed availability. Never move points speculatively. Virgin Atlantic charges high fuel surcharges on its own flights. You can be charged $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles for a Virgin-operated long-haul. This redemption only makes sense on ANA-operated flights, where the surcharge is zero. Confirm the operating carrier before you transfer anything.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This redemption is rated year-round, but ANA's award space to Japan tightens dramatically during cherry blossom season (late March–April), Golden Week (late April–early May), and December holidays. For the best combination of availability and experience, consider September–November or January–February travel.

The most efficient path to 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles is through Chase Ultimate Rewards (Chase Sapphire Preferred earns 3x on dining and travel; Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining) or Amex Membership Rewards (Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly with airlines). Both transfer 1:1 to Virgin Atlantic instantly.

This redemption is built for the couple or solo traveler who has been building a transferable points balance and is ready to make Japan the centerpiece of a bucket-list trip. If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it. You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

Ninety thousand miles gets you a private suite on a transpacific flight that costs $5,000-$8,000 in cash. The booking process requires patience and planning, particularly around the 331-day availability window, but the payoff is a genuinely world-class travel experience. If Japan is on your bucket list and you have been building transferable points, this is the redemption to target.

#8921. The Quintana Roo Service Course Studio NEXT Is a Serious Aero Race Bike

QR brings its triathlon roots to road with a configurable aero bike that clears 36mm tires.

Quintana Roo’s Service Course Studio NEXT is a mouthful of a name, but the idea is straightforward: a premium aero road bike from a brand with decades of triathlon experience. Its configurable build lets buyers choose more of the details up front than most race-bike brands allow.

That gives the Service Course a different starting point in a crowded category. I rode it to find out how QR’s triathlon instincts translate to road—and whether they give this bike a reason to stand out.

ACTUAL WEIGHT 17.6 lb. (size small, as tested)USE Road racing, fast group rides, fondos and centuriesPRICE AS TESTED $8,300 (estimated)MODEL PRICE RANGE $7,800 and upCUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS YesSIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, LCLAIMED FRAME WEIGHT 924g, painted size M with seatpost binder, without axles or headsetCLAIMED FORK WEIGHT 360gTIRE CLEARANCE 36mmBOTTOM BRACKET STANDARD T47DERAILLEUR HANGER UDHBRAKE HOSE ROUTING Fully internalWARRANTY Limited lifetime frame warranty for original owner

Quintana Roo Service Course Studio Next Gallery

The Service Course is QR’s aero road bike. Studio NEXT is its premium version, not a different frame concept or unique geometry. It uses the same frame shapes and fork as the standard model, with a higher-grade carbon layup that saves about 150 grams.

Brad DeVaney, QR’s lead engineer, told me the Studio NEXT frame uses more 46T carbon and less 30T fiber than the standard version. The internal mold components are similar, with adjustments to meet the weight target.

Like the standard Service Course, the Studio NEXT version is offered through QR’s online line configuration tool, which has multiple drivetrain, wheel, and other customization options. Additionally, QR will work with the customer to dial in gearing, crank length, and cockpit sizing. The Studio NEXT Service Course gets more premium paint options, painted logos instead of decals, and a few other different configuration options.

The Service Course has an extended headtube that comes to a prominent point, wide-set fork legs, dropped stays, and a deep downtube. Above the fork crown, a molded ridge QR calls a chine is designed to redirect air disturbed by the fork legs.

The bike clears tires up to 36mm. That doesn’t make it a gravel bike, but it does leave room to wider tires when conditions merit. The frame also uses a Universal Derailleur Hanger, threaded T47 bottom bracket, and non-proprietary upper headset bearing diameter that is compatible with several internal routing systems.

QR claims the painted size M Studio NEXT frame weighs 924 grams with the seatpost binder installed, but without axles or headset parts. QR also lists claimed weights of 360 grams for the fork and 240 grams for the seatpost with saddle hardware.

At 924 grams, the frame isn’t in the ultralight class. Specialized claims 687 grams for the S-Works Tarmac SL9 frame, and Trek lists 796 grams for a painted Madone SLR Gen 8 frame in size ML without hardware. Among dedicated aero frames, Canyon claims 960 grams for the Aeroad CFR.

These figures are rough context, not a clean ranking: frame size, paint, and included hardware vary between brands. Still, 924 grams is a competitive claim for an aero frame with clearance for 36mm tires.

Quintana Roo has run the Service Course in the wind tunnel, but it has been reticent to share specifics about the results or how the bike compares with its competitors. QR claims the Service Course is at least 3.6 watts faster than its previous SR-series road bike platform.

Not that I’d buy into QR’s data at face value even if it was provided. Data can be massaged and cherry-picked, and results can shift with the margin of error, bike-only versus rider-on-bike testing, bottle setup, wheels, tires, hood position, and more. Modern aero bikes can move up or down in a comparison depending on the protocol.

To QR’s credit, lead engineer Brad DeVaney gave me useful context. The relevant Service Course test used two standard water bottles. They also tested the Service Course with aero bottles, and it was, unsurprisingly, faster than it was with standard bottles, but DeVaney said they chose not to emphasize those results because most riders don’t use them.

DeVaney also said QR controlled handlebar stack and hood placement across comparison bikes, removed saddle position as a variable in non-rider testing, and used the SR as a calibration bike between test sessions.

That’s helpful. It still doesn’t answer the big question: How does the Service Course compare with the fastest aero road bikes from Specialized, Trek, Canyon, Cervélo, Giant, Factor, Pinarello, and the rest? QR says it has competitor data, but didn’t provide numbers I can publish.

So, is it aero? Yes. How aero? Much harder to say.

The frame has the hallmarks of a modern aero bike: a narrow, extended headtube; wide-set fork legs; a deep downtube; dropped stays; an aero seatpost; and aggressive shaping around the fork, headtube, and downtube. QR knows aerodynamics from its long history in triathlon.

And based on my riding, the Service Course feels like it punches through the air better than a non-aero bike. After decades of testing aero and non-aero bikes, that’s something I can usually feel.

I’m confident calling it competitively aero and likely on the faster side of the bell curve. I just can’t tell you where it sits in the current superbike hierarchy.

There’s a new split emerging in high-end race bike geometry.

On one side are bikes like the Factor One, Ridley Noah Fast 3.0, Ridley Falcn RS 2.0, and Eddy Merckx 525R. These aren’t simply aero frames with hidden hoses and deep tubes. They’re built around a forward, hoods-primary riding position: the rider shifts forward relative to the bottom bracket and stretches farther over the hoods. The geometry aims to preserve balance and handling as the rider’s mass shifts forward.

Factor is particularly explicit about this with the One. Ridley and Eddy Merckx describe similar goals for their newer race bikes, including steeper seat angles and longer reaches.

The Service Course is not that kind of bike, at least not on paper.

That’s interesting because Quintana Roo is a triathlon-first company. A forward road-racing position has a lot in common with a triathlon position, and QR has spent decades thinking about aerodynamics, rider position, and how to make the rider faster when the body is the biggest thing in the wind. If any brand had permission to push harder on forward-position road bike geometry, it’s QR.

So I’m surprised the Service Course’s geometry is not more progressive. Its fit is closer to a modern traditional road-race bike like the Trek Madone or Specialized Tarmac than to the Factor, Ridley, and Eddy Merckx bikes above.

That doesn’t mean you can’t set up the QR for a forward position. The 0mm-offset seatpost, saddle-rail adjustment, crank-length choices, and cockpit options give the user room to dial in that kind of position. But being able to set up a bike for a forward position isn’t the same as designing the frame around one.

The newer forward-fit bikes build that position into the chassis: their seat angles, reach, front centers, cockpit layouts, and handling are designed around a rider moving forward, using shorter cranks and narrower bars, and spending more time on the hoods. The goal is to preserve balance and handling as the rider’s mass shifts forward.

That isn’t automatically better. Traditional road geometry is familiar and easier to fit, and it may avoid some handling compromises that can come from moving a rider forward on a chassis and altering the handling geometry around that weight shift.

DeVaney pushed back on my read. He said a more forward position was part of its design foundation. He also pointed to QR’s 0mm- and 20mm-offset seatpost options as evidence that the bike is intended to cover a broad range of race positions.

Still, I can’t help wondering what QR does next. A Service Course V2 that leans harder into the company’s triathlon DNA and the latest forward-fit thinking could get very interesting.

One other geometry detail: the Service Course is offered in only four sizes: extra-small, small, medium, and large. Most high-end frames come in six or more sizes.

Because QR uses a configurator, the Service Course Studio NEXT does not fit neatly into the usual “this model comes with these parts and costs this much” box.

That configurator is one of the more interesting things about buying a QR. Beyond the choices you can click on, you can specify details like gearing and crank length instead of immediately planning your first round of upgrades.

At the time I’m writing this, the Service Course Studio NEXT builds start at $7,800 with Ultregra Di2 with 4iiii power meter, DT Swiss ARC 1600 Dicut wheels, and a Vision Metron 5D ACR EVO integrated cockpit.

Note that the current configurator differs from the one I used when I built my review bike. The biggest difference is that, at that time, SRAM Force AXS was an option, and now it isn't. Based on the assumption that a Force AXS build is slightly more expensive than Ultegra Di2 with power meter build, I’m estimating my review bike’s price is about $8,300

The current QR configurator offers Shimano Ultegra, Shimano Dura-Ace, and SRAM RED builds, with wheel options including Zipp, DT Swiss, ENVE, and HED. Current tire options include Continental GP5000 and Vittoria Corsa Pro and Corsa Pro Control tires.

But as I found out, the configuration tool changes, so available options come and go. But QR encourages customers to reach out with off-menu requests, so you can contact their team for component requests not shown in the configurator.

The Service Course Studio NEXT lands in one of the most competitive parts of the road market: the high-end race bike.

That means it is up against the obvious big-brand machines from Specialized, Trek, Giant, Cannondale, Canyon, Cervélo, Scott, BMC, Factor, Pinarello, and others. Some have more racing visibility. Some have larger dealer networks. Some have more frame sizes. Some are lighter.

The Service Course Studio NEXT gives you a claimed 924g painted aero frame, 36mm tire clearance, UDH, T47A, a claimed service-friendly headset, and a much more customizable buying experience than most major brands offer.

The rider who wants a WorldTour-shaped object with a massive dealer network probably already knows where they are going. The rider who wants a fast aero road bike but also wants to choose bar width, stem length, crank length, saddle, wheels, tires, color, and cockpit before the bike ships should look harder at QR.

QR has credibility—just not the usual road credibility. In triathlon, the brand’s history means something. In road, it still has to prove itself to riders who reflexively reach for the familiar names.

Whether that matters is up to the buyer. It should not matter more than the bike. But bikes are emotional objects, and logo gravity is real.

The Quintana Roo Service Course Studio NEXT, hereafter the SCSN to save my fingers from an overuse injury, met all my expectations for a modern, high-end race bike.

It feels quick, moves efficiently, has light and precise handling, and offers a reasonably compliant ride while transmitting appropriate feedback to the rider.

I did find it a little loud. Road noise, shifting, and braking are amplified by the frame, which isn’t surprising for a stiff frame with big tubes.

Some of the race bikes I’ve been riding concurrently, like the Tarmac and Madone, have smaller tubes and don’t pick up and amplify as much noise. The SCSN is even a bit louder than the Canyon Aeroad CFR, another bike in the same full-aero category.

It was loudest with the HED 62mm wheels that came with my test bike, but I fitted several other wheelsets to the SCSN and it remained louder than average.

I am a fan of quiet bikes, so I’m admittedly more persnickety about noise than many riders. Take that for what it’s worth.

Other than the noise, I have few complaints about the SCSN. In a very competitive category, it holds its own admirably well.

I was particularly impressed by its cornering performance and high-speed handling. One of my favorite test loops ends with a descent that starts with a steep, dead-straight section alongside a reservoir before diving into a canyon with several turns of varying radius and not-great pavement. Between the reservoir and canyon, the wind is usually unpredictably gusty and swirly.

I take all my test bikes down this road at least once, so I’ve built up a good mental basis for comparison. The SCSN was one of the best I’ve ever taken down it.

Despite its aero profile, it was rock solid when I was supertucked at more than 50 mph. When I returned to the saddle for the canyon turns, I immediately noticed how smoothly the SCSN initiated each turn, finding that intuitive balance between too quick and twitchy and too stable and sluggish.

But what really impressed me was how well it tracked through the turns. Between the wind and changing pavement, there is a lot here that can upset a bike, which is unsettling when speeds are above 40 mph, cars are climbing in the other lane, and I’m trying to navigate around potholes and sand washed onto the road. It’s a complex and potentially dangerous section of pavement, which isn’t helped by my need to try to set a PR every time.

And damn, did the SCSN carve these corners and prove itself a worthy companion in the chaos like few bikes I’ve ridden.

If you are wondering, no, I did not PR the segment on the SCSN. After so many attempts, getting that PR now feels as much a matter of catching the right wind and traffic as it does of riding a great-handling bike. Still, I do feel a new PR is within reach on the SCSN if the conditions line up, which is more than I can say about some bikes.

Rider comfort and compliance were also better than I anticipated, with the front and rear feeling well balanced. I will note, however, that because of my fit and Quintana Roo’s sizing, I was riding the size small frame with the seatpost at its extension limit.

So, yes, I found the SCSN to be a very good bike. Above average, for sure.

And I want to again shout out QR for the no-fuss customizability it offers. I also love the little details the Studio NEXT program brings, like painting the handlebar and transition spacers to match the frame. That is an uncommon and very premium touch.

But I get hung up when I try to answer the question: Why buy this bike instead of the many other great race bikes you can buy from brands big and small?

Certainly, the customization is a boon, but you can find that from Factor and Trek through Project One, among others. The SCSN rides and handles well, but I’d say the Tarmac is a more refined package on this front. It’s competitively aerodynamic, but I can almost guarantee the Cervélo S5 is markedly more slippery. It’s a good value, but brands like X-Lab, Winspace, and Quick Pro soundly beat it on that front. And Quintana Roo doesn’t have a vibe that lets you flex at the group-ride meetup.

I’m not trying to slam Quintana Roo here, and apologies to anyone there who feels like I am. It’s just that the market is awash in so many fast race bikes, many of them very good, that it becomes really difficult for me, as an objective—but human—reviewer and recommender of bikes, to arrive at the SCSN as the race bike someone should buy if they’re shopping right now.

And, to be totally fair to QR, I could say the same thing about many other bikes.

Ultimately, what you buy is your decision. So I’ll close with this: The SCSN is a great bike from a brand that knows a lot about building bikes made to go fast.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.
