#8919. This Self-Coached Data Scientist Had Never Run a Marathon Before. Then He Won NYC.

Andreas Almgren made his marathon debut on the streets of New York this weekend—and he won in 2:06:01.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published on October 27, 2026. At the NYC Marathon on November 1, Almgren gapped the field and won the race in 2:06:01.

When the elites line up for the New York City Marathon on November 1, there will be a mix of former winners, Olympic medalists, and two of the top American marathoners in the country, Conner Mantz and Zouhair Talbi.

Looking to spoil the party will be Andreas Almgren, a 31-year-old Swedish runner who won the World Half Marathon Championships in September. This will be Almgren’s debut at the 26.2-mile distance. Despite his inexperience, he’s a legitimate threat for the podium.

Almgren has an unconventional background as a pro runner. He was working as a data scientist just two years ago. He mostly trains alone and coaches himself. But he’s far from a competitive amateur. He’s sponsored by Nike and has set European records in the road 10K (26:45) and half marathon (58:06).

Although his strengths have been on the track and shorter road events, Almgren has leaned fully into marathon training this fall, logging more than 135 miles a week and tackling long runs over 24 miles. He says he’s well-prepared heading into New York.

“I’m actually feeling really confident,” Almgren told Runner’s World ahead of the race. “I might be a bit naive, but the training has gone really well. I’ve done a few really good workouts. But the marathon is a different beast. You don’t really know until you're reaching that 35K mark if you're going to make it or not. But I’m feeling really good.”

Here are six things to know about Almgren ahead of his marathon debut in New York City.

Almgren first made a splash on the world scene as an 800-meter specialist, earning bronze in the event at the World Junior Championships in 2014. For about a decade, he was coached by Urban Aruhn, but around 2019, Almgren began experimenting with Norwegian threshold training and gradually started to create his own training plans.

Aruhn is still involved today, but in a more general role. Before a training cycle, Almgren will run his plan by Aruhn, who plays “devil’s advocate,” trying to poke holes in it or prod Almgren to explain his reasoning.

“If we disagree on something, then we discuss it,” Almgren said. “But in the end, it’s in my hands.”

Before he was a full-time professional runner, Almgren worked as a risk analyst at a financial company and then as a data scientist for the sports tech software company Svexa. It wasn’t until he was sidelined from the 2024 Olympics with a stress fracture that he decided to quit his job and focus on running full-time.

Now, Almgren—who has a bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering and management and has taken graduate coursework in mathematics, optimization, and systems theory—scratches that itch by rigorously tracking his training metrics.

“I like data,” he said. “And I collect basically the things that I think are important for every workout.”

Almgren has an Excel spreadsheet where he logs every workout and numerous data points: interval times, heart rate readings, blood lactate measurements, etc. The spreadsheet data goes back to 2012, and Almgren will look back on past sessions to inform his current training.

Almgren has been preparing for New York with an altitude stint in Flagstaff, Arizona, which sits 7,000 feet above sea level. He’s also introduced heat training during some of his training blocks, and he looks to sports like cycling and speed skating for cutting-edge training methods.

About two years ago, Almgren started experimenting with Nomio, a broccoli sprout extract shot that is quickly catching on among elite runners. Nomio claims the product can reduce lactate during hard efforts and accelerate recovery.

Almgren, who is sponsored by the brand, said it helps keep his legs feeling fresh during intervals.

“I just feel like I can train harder than I did before and more and still recover from it,” he said. “Run a little bit faster on my threshold workouts and everything. So I think if you get those tiny margins over and over, day by day, I think that could help quite a lot.”

Almgren knew he wanted to race a marathon in the fall of 2026, but he didn’t want to sacrifice a full track season before diving into marathon training. He chose New York because it gave him time to recover from the track season, and he wanted to find an honest race, compared to a more time-oriented flat course like Spain’s Valencia Marathon in December.

“In a time trial, I wouldn’t really know what time to aim for,” Almgren said. “There’s a big risk that I blow up. If I’m going in Valencia, you have Yomif [Kejelcha] and John Korir taking off in probably sub-two-hour pace, and I’m not going to follow that. So I think that New York is a better race for me with inexperience, just trying to stay in the front pack and see what can happen.”

Oftentimes, pro runners will “move to the marathon,” implying their days of barreling around the track are over. But Almgren wants to do both. He fully intends to run a track season in 2027, and, looking ahead to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, he believes the 10,000 meters could be his best event.

If Almgren finishes in the top five at New York, he will earn the Olympic standard and pave the path for a spot on the Swedish marathon team for the upcoming Games.

Only Emil Zatopek has won gold in the 10,000 meters and marathon at the same Olympics.

Like most elite runners who race the hilly New York course, Almgren doesn’t care what his finishing time is on November 1. Instead, he wants to run with the top group as long as he can.

“The goal is to be in the mindset that I should try to be able to compete for the whole race,” he said. “I don't want to, let’s say, chicken out at 30K. I want to try to be in it for as long as possible. And if that means that I blow up at 37K, then so be it.

“But I hope that I should be able to be in the mix up until Central Park and hopefully even maybe come out on top. We’ll see. You should never underestimate a marathon. And I don’t have the experience, so I don’t know what’s going to happen, but I’m going to try to be in the mix.”

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.)

#8918. This $16 Tool Can Save You Thousands of Dollars Across the Life Span of Your Bike

Catch chain wear early and you could save hundreds—or more—on drivetrain replacements.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I’ve checked in thousands of bikes for service, and I used to hear this line all the time: “I ride the bike a lot, but it’s in great shape. The shifting just jumps around a little.” Once I would get to the step of putting a chain checker on the chain, that $16 tool might tell the story of hundreds of dollars in upcoming repairs.

A chain checker was one of my most recommended service tools to customers when I ran a bike shop service department. The key is to make sure you are buying the correct one and understand how to use it. The chain checker most shops I worked in was the Park Tool CC2 —the chain checker with the swivel dial.

This option was great because it gave customers and service advisors an easy visual on the wear level of a chain. But the biggest reason my favorite chain checker isn’t this one is because it does not give a clear reading on certain SRAM chains. Read on to find out which chain checker I suggest, why it can save you thousands of dollars across the life span of your bike, and how to use this small tool.

When a chain gets stretched it can cause issues like slow shifting, unexpected chain jumps, and the chain can have a slipping feeling under power. Sometimes these issues can also be mistaken for cable tension being off in a derailleur, but you can easily check the chain stretch at home if you have this chain checker.

It is extremely difficult to tell how worn a drivetrain is with the naked eye. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. My favorite chain checker is the Pedro’s Chain Checker because it is compatible with most chain makes and models. It also retails for only $16 and it is small enough to fit in almost anyone’s tool roll or kit.

Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn. If the chain is over 75 percent worn that recommendation changes to replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) when it measures over 100 percent worn. Typically 10-speed chains and lower have a bigger tolerance to stretch, with singlespeeds having the biggest acceptable stretch.

Many times a customer would ask if the shop could just throw a new chain onto a drivetrain that is past that 100 percent mark. If you do this, the shifting can actually get worse because the wear pattern in the new chain no longer lines up with the wear pattern on the existing cassette and chainrings. An even worse case scenario of putting a new chain on a worn drivetrain is chain suck. This is when a worn chainring can get stuck to the chain from the bottom of the pedal stroke. Then the chain gets sucked up and jammed between the chainring and the frame—possibly leading to damage on the frame. Once a drivetrain has a certain level of wear replacing only one part of the system does not work.

The price for some higher-end cassettes can range anywhere from $400 to $660 from brands like Shimano and SRAM. I go by a three-strike rule with chains (spokes too, but that’s a different story). For my own bikes I typically get three chains out of each cassette.

If you are on top of chain wear with a chain checker, this could save you almost $2,000 in cassette costs alone when using high-end SRAM cassettes. Remember, this price doesn’t include labor or the cost of chainrings—which you’ll need to replace if you keep running the chain until it’s above that 100 percent wear mark.

Some higher-end chainrings, like the SRAM Red direct-mount chainring, can run up to almost $300 per ring. If someone runs the whole drivetrain into the ground, then a checkup for shifting issues can quickly turn into a thousand-dollar bill on a high end drivetrain. If you’re running Shimano 105 or SRAM Rival, then being on top of chain wear might not save you thousands as quickly as running the highest end group set. Rest assured, overtime you’ll get there too. The better news is that Pedro's chain checker is so easy to use.

Start by dropping the tooth with the number one above it into the chain. Once the number one tooth is dropped in, then drop the tooth with the number two above it into the chain. Finally, try to drop the third tooth (numbered with a three) into the chain. If this tooth doesn’t drop in through the links in the chain, then good news! Your chain is less than 50 percent worn. If it drops halfway through the chain that means your chain is about 75 percent worn. Finally, if the tooth numbered three on the chain checker drops all the way through the chain that means it is between 75 percent and 100 percent worn. Typically I suggest if you have 11, 12, or 13 speed chains around that 50 percent worn mark change the chain soon to keep the rest drivetrain alive as long as possible.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. #8917. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8915. Is Cycling Good Cardio? Here's How It Compares to Running and Swimming

Learn how cycling compares to other cardio activities like walking, running, and swimming.

Riding a bike is as good a workout as it is a ton of fun. Hop on a bike—any kind—and your heart rate will pick up, your breathing rate will increase, and you’ll break a sweat. Whether you choose to fly over asphalt on a road bike, cruise back roads on a gravel setup, or push pedals in an indoor studio, you’re doing your mind and body big favors when you hop in the saddle.

One of the biggest payoffs? Cardio benefits. Read on for how cycling boosts your cardio fitness and how it stacks up to other forms of cardiovascular exercise, like running and using an elliptical.

Cardio exercise is any exercise that increases your heart rate and respiration (breathing rate). Cardio exercise can be aerobic or anaerobic. Broadly, what makes cardio aerobic or anaerobic is the intensity level of the exercise (and physiologically, the source of energy for that exercise).

Aerobic exercise, defined by the American College of Sports Medicine, is a rhythmic activity that uses large muscle groups and can be maintained continuously. This is also called steady-state exercise, and it can include running, walking, cycling, rowing, using the elliptical or stair-stepper, swimming, and hiking.

Anaerobic cardio exercise is high-intensity, and true anaerobic activity can only be performed for short periods of time; sprinting is a good example of anaerobic cardio exercise. Activities like jumping rope and mountain biking—and any of the aforementioned activities performed in high-intensity spurts—can also fit into this cardio category.

In any case, “cardio exercise often consists of extended periods of time with an elevated heart rate and an increase in oxygen demand,” says Alexander Rothstein, ACSM-certified exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning coach, and coordinator for the exercise science program at New York Institute of Technology.

“Performing cardio exercise will stress the cardiovascular system, which will signal the need for adaptation and cause improvements in the body’s ability to supply and utilize oxygen,” he explains.

The goal of cardio exercise is to increase the efficiency of your heart, lungs, and circulatory system, thereby improving your overall fitness and endurance.

“Cardiorespiratory fitness reflects the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen-rich blood to skeletal muscles during sustained physical activity,” says Joe Scarrella, triathlon coach and certified personal trainer at Life Time Chanhassen in Minnesota.

This type of fitness “is vitally important to health and wellness, especially to the ability of engaging in normal activities of daily living without excessive fatigue,” he says. “Because of its heart-strengthening and overall health benefits, cardio training should always be near the top of priorities when allocating time to a fitness program.”

Yes, cycling is cardio exercise—an excellent form of it, in fact. Cycling requires continuous movement that increases your heart rate. When you pedal, your heart works harder to pump blood to your muscles. This steady effort challenges your cardiovascular system, helping it become more efficient over time.

A cycling habit brings about a lot of benefits, including:

While cycling is a fantastic form of cardio, it’s not your only option. Here’s a look at how it measures up to other popular forms of cardio exercise.

Cycling burns more calories per hour than walking, according to the Compendium of Physical Activity. Cycling at a leisurely pace (less than 10 mph) can burn about 330 calories per hour for a 180-pound person. Walking at a leisurely pace (2.5 mph) burns about 246 calories per hour for a person of the same weight.

Both cycling and walking are low-impact exercises, making them ideal for those with joint pain or arthritis. Cycling allows more room for increasing speed or resistance without changing joint impact, which offers a more intense cardio workout for individuals with joint concerns.

On the flip side, walking is a weight-bearing form of exercise, while cycling is not, so walking could be the better choice for individuals with bone density concerns.

Walking is more accessible because it requires no equipment beyond a good pair of shoes. Cycling, on the other hand, requires much more gear: a bike and helmet, at minimum, plus safe space to ride outdoors. An indoor stationary bike or bike trainer is required for cycling inside, and while there are budget options, it’s still an investment.

If you're looking for a simple, accessible form of low-intensity cardio, walking might be the best option. However, for a more intense workout that’s still easy on the joints, cycling is the way to go.

Running tends to burn more calories than cycling, because it’s more difficult for many individuals to achieve the increase in heart rate that they may get from running, Rothstein says. It may take longer to burn as many calories as one would while running.

According to data from the Compendium of Physical Activity, cycling at a “self-selected moderate pace” burns about 573 calories in one hour for a 180-pound person. That same person may burn about 615 calories “jogging at a self-selected pace,” according to the Compendium.

Running is a high-impact exercise, which can place stress on your joints, especially your knees and ankles. Cycling, in contrast, is low-impact, making it a better option for people with joint issues or those recovering from injuries.

Both running and cycling primarily work your lower body, including your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. During cycling, your core and back muscles may be recruited more to maintain posture on the bike, depending on the style of your bike. When running, your core, back, and arms all work to maintain posture and stability.

If joint health is a concern or you prefer a lower-impact workout, cycling is the better choice. Running is a viable option for people who can handle the joint impact and/or don’t have the means to invest in a bike or stationary bike.

Swimming and cycling burn similar amounts of calories, depending on intensity. According to the Compendium of Physical Activity, swimming freestyle at a vigorous pace for one hour burns about 800 calories for a 180-pound person. The same person would burn about 818 calories cycling at 14 to 16 mph, which may be a moderate or vigorous effort depending on your fitness level.

Swimming has virtually no impact on joints because the water supports your body, making it an ideal option for those with joint pain, injuries, or mobility issues.

Cycling is also low-impact but not quite as easy on the body as swimming. Depending on the type of bike, some individuals may struggle with mobility when cycling. (For example, on a road bike with drop bars, it can strain the neck and back to reach them. In such a case, a bike with an upright frame might be a better choice.)

Swimming is a full-body workout, engaging both your upper and lower body, as well as your core. You’ll recruit more muscles in the arms and shoulders while swimming, compared to cycling, which primarily targets the lower body.

If you want a no-impact, full-body workout, swimming might be your best option. Keep in mind that sticking to a swimming plan requires having access to a lap pool, which isn’t feasible for everyone. Even though a bike can be a big investment, it may be the more accessible option in this case.

Cycling burns more calories than elliptical training at the same effort level. For a 180-pound person, cycling at a moderate pace (12 to 14 mph) burns around 654 calories in 60 minutes, while a moderate 60-minute session on the elliptical burns about 409 calories.

Both are low-impact exercises, making them suitable for people with joint concerns. The elliptical may provide an advantage for people who struggle with mobility, because you remain in an upright position and don’t have to significantly flex the spine like on the bike.

Elliptical machines engage both the upper and lower body, while cycling primarily focuses on your lower body, though the upper body and core are still engaged to some extent while riding a bike.

If you prefer a workout that engages your whole body, the elliptical may be the better choice. However, if you like the idea of getting outside and/or exercising with a community, cycling offers a more dynamic experience in that sense.

Overall, “all forms of cardio are similar in their cardiovascular health and weight loss benefits,” says Rothstein. “The increased oxygen demand and overall cardiovascular stress will result in improved health and well-being. The ability to burn calories is also similar even if the rate might be different between types of cardio.”

Adaptations in stamina are where the most significant differences lie, says Rothstein. “We adapt based on the specific training stimulus, so in cyclists, stamina improvements will mostly be shown in cycling performance. For example, if you train cycling, you will not improve your running unless you also train as a runner. This is because even though both have cardiovascular adaptation benefits, the muscular adaptations will be specific to the type of training.”

In other words: Train what you want to be good at doing.

#8914. Choosing a Gravel Bike? These 12 Editor-Tested Models Deliver the Tire Clearance, Geometry, and Value That Matter

From bikepacking to gravel racing, these tested bikes cover every kind of dirt-road ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Instead of riding busy, congested city and suburban roads, many cyclists now head to lightly traveled gravel and unimproved roads. Gravel riding is a great way to see beautiful fall foliage, enjoy the fresh air, and avoid traffic. Most brands sell at least one gravel model; some offer multiple gravel platforms or bikes designed for particular gravel-riding niches. Whether you need a new bicycle for a big gravel fondo or race, a versatile bike for multi-surface rides, or a rig for bikepacking adventures, there’s a gravel bike for you.

The term “gravel riding” is very broad and doesn’t necessarily mean riding on gravel surfaces the entire ride. Gravel rides can include anything from hard-packed dirt roads (which you can often ride on a traditional road bike) to singletrack trails (typically associated with mountain bikes). Gravel riding also includes almost any other type of unimproved roadway; forest access roads, farm roads, jeep roads, rail trails, and canal paths are all commonly lumped under the gravel umbrella. And many of the best gravel routes and events incorporate a few of these surfaces.

Because they get ridden in such varied terrain, gravel bikes come in many shapes and sizes. They span the gamut of aero-optimized bikes that look similar to WorldTour road bikes to full suspension models that resemble mountain bikes with dropbars—But most gravel bikes fall somewhere in between these polar extremes. Most gravel bikes share a few key traits: Generous tire clearance, a more upright riding position, and geometry that prioritizes stability and confidence on rough surfaces.

Buying Tip: Don’t pass on a great gravel bike because you don’t like its tires. Focus on a bike’s tire clearance rather than the stock rubber’s tread or width. Brands usually equip gravel bikes with tires that work well in average conditions. If those tires don’t work for you, it’s a simple fix. Upgrading to tires that better suit your needs is often the best—and easiest—first change you can make, and it usually shaves weight.

The Canyon Grizl is a great all-arounder. It’s a gravel bike built for all sorts of adventures, whether it’s a casual after-work gravel spin, commuting around town, or a multi-day bikepacking trip. The SRAM Apex XPLR 1x12 drivetrain shifts quickly and has a wide gear range. The Grizl’s carbon frame also helps dampen the bumps on rougher roads and trails.

Since we tested the bike a few seasons ago, platform updates have improved its capability and appeal. The Grizl now features clearance for wider tires (up to 56mm), internal downtube storage, and an easily sourced UDH hanger. If this model doesn't speak to you, Canyon offers several Grizl options priced from $1,899 to $4,699.

If you don’t have thousands of dollars to spend but need a bike for riding actual gravel roads, your choices might seem limited. However, if you dig into brands’ websites and look for budget picks, you will find a few gems. The $1,300 Salsa Journeyer Essa is a good example; it stands out for its robust parts, wide tires, and size range.

Unlike some cheaper gravel bikes you may find on Amazon, the Journeyer’s aluminum frame comes in six sizes to fit riders from 4’8” to 6’5”. Additionally, it’s available through REI. This way, you’ll have warranty support if anything goes awry, and the bike is professionally assembled (if you choose in-store pickup).

For components, Salsa equips this Journeyer model with Shimano’s 1x8-speed Essa group (including Shimano mechanical disc brakes)—the parts aren’t fancy, but they’re robust. The only negative point of the Journeyer Essa is its standard QR dropouts, which make upgrading to lighter-weight or tubeless wheels slightly more difficult.

The Topstone 1 is Cannondale’s top-tier aluminum gravel bike. Designed for versatility and adventure, it’s equally at home on pavement or dirt, with a utilitarian setup that includes mounts for racks, bags, fenders, and extra bottles—perfect for long-haul rides. But don’t mistake utilitarian for boring; the Topstone still feels lively and efficient on the road, making it a great choice for days when your rides lean more toward pavement.

This model comes with 37mm tires, but the frame clears up to 45mm rubber. This allows you to choose tires for the terrain and rides you take. The Shimano GRX 2x11 drivetrain is another standout, offering a wide gear range for steep, rough climbs while keeping gear jumps tight—something you’ll appreciate when riding extended stretches of pavement.

Salsa practically invented the modern gravel bike with its Warbird, and the Minnesota-based brand remains as relevant as ever. Its recently launched Flyway C is a lightweight and responsive gravel bike for gravel racing or all-day rides. It features generous tire clearance (up to 57mm), a UDH dropout (for easy replacement or upgrades), and revised geometry (long reach and short stem) for improved control on rough terrain.

Several Flyway configurations are available (I tested the Force AXS XPLR model), and I think the Apex Eagle AXS model sits right in the sweet spot for many riders. As the name suggests, Salsa outfits this bike with a combination of SRAM’s Apex AXS and Eagle X1 AXS 1x electronic drivetrains to provide a superwide gear range. In addition to the great components, Salsa also equips this model with a flared carbon bar and a carbon seatpost. It’s an all-around great package for anyone looking to up their gravel game this season.

Trek’s Checkpoint ALR 5 is versatile, well-rounded, and a great pick for riders new to gravel cycling. In his review, Chabanov says, “The value sweet spot: modern geometry and feature set borrowed from the [Checkpoint] SL, delivered in a durable alloy package with smart mounts and standards—at a starting price that leaves room in the budget for meaningful upgrades. Because there are no proprietary parts, upgrading and swapping things like the handlebar, stem, and seatpost is super easy.”

Overall, the Checkpoint ALR gets far more right than it gets wrong. Sure, you can nitpick the stock wheels and tires—or wish for the carbon model’s downtube storage and IsoSpeed—but those trade-offs help keep the price in check while preserving what matters. This bike has confident handling, generous tire room, real-world durability, and an upgrade-friendly platform. The result is a thoroughly well-thought-out aluminum gravel bike that feels ready for anything from weeknight dirt spins to loaded weekend overnighters, or even that gravel race that’s on your bucket list.

If you’re a gravel racer on a budget, or simply like going fast and don’t have the money for bikes like the Specialized S-Works Crux or Colnago G5-X, Canyon’s new Grail should be on your short list. As my colleague Matt Phillips described in his review of the revised platform, “And “fast” was the word that stuck with me as I rode the Grail across singletrack, dirt roads, and paved roads. It feels fast. It made me feel like I was fast.”

Wide tire clearance is one of the latest Grail’s upgrade highlights. At 57mm, the frame and fork can fit the widest gravel tires and even 29 x 2.25-inch mountain bike rubber for rocky terrain or singletrack (or if you want a super comfortable feel). The entry-tier Grail CF SL models use a heavier carbon frame than the Grail CFR and CF SLX versions, but only 140 grams more than the high-end CFR bike (about the weight of a standard butyl inner tube). All models feature a carbon cockpit, seatpost, and wheels.

The Grail CF 7 Speed is a great bang-for-the-buck gravel racer. Canyon equips it with SRAM’s excellent Rival XPLR AXS 1x13 electronic shifting gravel groupset. Although Canyon doesn’t ship this model with a power meter, you can easily upgrade to a Rival power crank for under $200.

You’re not buying this bike for its tire clearance, gear-hauling options, or aerodynamics; plenty of other gravel bikes do those things better than the G5-X. You buy this bike because it’s a Colnago.

On fast gravel roads, double track, and even technical singletrack, Colnago’s superb geometry, fit, and ride comfort won me over. The G5-X feels super composed and planted when descending and over choppy gravel road sections. The bike is precise and refined—pick your line and take it. On climbs and rolling terrain, the G5-X is comfortable and efficient, and responds immediately to bursts of power.

Overall, Colnago’s latest bike is a beautifully fast gravel racer with sublime handling. However, while the G5-X has more tire clearance (53mm) than the brand’s previous gravel offerings, it falls a few millimeters shy of the clearance found on some new gravel models. This will matter to some, but many riders will seek out the G5-X for the name on the downtube and Colnago’s cycling legacy.

Inspired by the Tour Divide—America’s longest mountain bike race—this bike carries more and handles a wider range of terrain than almost any other gravel bike. It’s loaded with mounts for racks, camping gear, bike accessories, and water bottles.

Although it’s intended for burly rides, the Cutthroat features a carbon frame and fork, which helps to reduce weight. And Salsa’s Class 5 Vibration Reduction System absorbs uneven terrain for a more comfortable ride. The Cutthroat C GRX model also includes a Shimano GRX 1x12 mechanical, wide-range drivetrain and a dropper seatpost.

With its steel frame, bar-end shifters, and triple-chainring crankset, the Masi Giramondo is a throwback to a bygone era of bicycle design and construction. While the bike’s aesthetic and features might not appeal to athletes chasing fast finishing times in 200-mile gravel races, it’s perfect for riders who want to hit the gravel, dirt, or paved roads loaded down with gear for touring adventures.

Unlike most bikes sold for touring or bikepacking, the Giramondo comes stock with a front and rear rack. This means you won’t have to add them to your bike-buying budget. To make it slightly easier to pedal your fully laden bike up hills, Masi equips this model with a triple crankset. While triples aren’t as trendy as 1x drivetrains, they offer an extremely wide gear range: Its lowest gear is close to many mountain bikes, and the highest gear rivals many gravel race bikes.

While State labels this model “All-Road,” it’s very much a modern gravel bike. Starting at $2,400 for a complete bike, or $1,400 for the frameset, the All-Road Carbon checks all of the boxes without totally draining your bank account. It accommodates up to 2.2-inch tires (complete builds ship with 50mm Vittoria T50s), is UDH-compatible, and takes a T47 bottom bracket. The All-Road Carbon also features internal storage in the frame’s downtube with a Fidlock magnetic latch.

The Carbon All-Road’s frame isn’t super aero-shaped, and it doesn’t use funky proprietary parts—and that’s a good thing. This bike is made for riders who prioritize durability and functionality over flashy graphics, pro teams, and marketing hype. The All-Road’s geometry falls on the “race-inspired” end of the spectrum, compared with the more upright feel of adventure-style gravel bikes. The bike carries speed on hardpack dirt and gravel and feels adequately stiff when sprinting and out of corners. The ride quality is a little harsher than premium gravel offerings, but a complete Carbon All-Road costs less than most big-name brands’ frames.

The all-new Specialized Crux has shed its cyclocross roots and turned into a modern gravel racer. In his review of the fifth-generation platform, Test Editor Dan Chabanov says, “It is built around the demands of professional gravel racers, and around the idea that going fast off-road now means balancing low weight, aero efficiency, tire clearance, and stability rather than just chasing the lightest possible frame.” The result is an excellent gravel bike that, while optimized for racers, anyone who loves going fast can enjoy.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips rode the Crux 5 for several days on the gravel roads in Durango, Colorado, and walked away very impressed by the updated bike. “The Crux 5 leans more toward stability and predictability,” he said. “It’s fast, yes. Very fast. But it’s also composed. It lets you settle in. It doesn’t feel like it’s trying to prove something every second.”

That balance is a big part of what makes the Crux great for non-racers. “A lot of us don’t need a gravel bike that only makes sense at 300 watts,” Phillips said. “We need a bike that feels sharp when you want to go hard, but isn’t a pain in the ass the rest of the time.”

Of the five models in the Crux 5 lineup, the Crux 5 Comp stands out for its performance-to-price ratio. It features a slightly heavier carbon frame than the high-end S-Works variants, but it has the same great geometry, tire clearance, and aerodynamics. Specialized equips the Comp model with SRAM’s excellent Rival AXS XPLR 1x brakes and drivetrain, and the bike rolls on 26mm-wide inner diameter alloy wheels wrapped in 45mm-wide Pathfinder tubeless tires.

The bike used by two-time gravel World Champion Marianne Vos (🐐), the Áspero-5 is what happens when Cervélo combines aerodynamic principles of the Paris-Roubaix-winning S5 with a gravel race bike. This bike is eye-wateringly fast on smoother gravel and dirt roads. The Áspero-5 is fast enough that many riders will want to use it on paved roads too.

Much of this speed advantage comes from Cervélo’s aerodynamic tuning of the frame, fork, and bar; the 42mm-wide Vittoria Corsa Pro Control TLR rubber enhances it. An excellent road tire for broken pavement in narrow sizes, the Pro Control really shines in the 700x42c size on dirt and gravel surfaces.

With so many types and sub-niches of gravel bikes, it can seem overwhelming to pick the right one. My first advice: start by honestly evaluating the terrain you ride, then consider how you like to ride it. From there, narrow your choices to the bikes that meet your budget, personal tastes, and other factors.

Racing-oriented bikes typically feature an aggressive fit and handling with fewer mounts for bags or extra water bottles. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes built for long-distance, multi-day adventures, equipped with all the mounts you could want for gear and accessories. In between, there’s a wide range of subtle variations that can make a big difference.

8-week plan to take your cycling to the next level

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8911. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8910. 5 Signs You’ve Graduated From Beginner Cyclist Status

“When did you first realize you weren’t a beginner anymore?”

It’s a question I posed to my coworkers at Bicycling, many of whom have been riding and racing for multiple decades, at elite levels, across staggering distances, possibly uphill both ways in the snow.

I expected my inbox to be flooded with inspiring anecdotes; tales of triumph and woe; or at the very least, smug hot takes on when it’s OK to start caring about insider stuff like embro and VO2 Max.

But such was not the case. “Oh, I still feel like a beginner almost every day,” was the almost universal, almost completely BS response.

While I admired the humility, based on how many times my colleagues have teased me about my sock height alone, I knew all that self-effacement was completely false. So I pushed back, and eventually they coughed up a few earnest responses.

In many ways, they’re right—it’s great to never lose that wide-eyed rookie sense of discovery and fun. But it’s also pretty cool to see those little glimpses of progress along the way.

If you’re anything like us, here’s how you might have guessed you were starting to get a handle on this whole bicycle-riding thing, no matter how much chain grease might be stamped across your calves.

#8908. Ciara Mageean, Irish 1500-Meter Champion and Olympian, Dies at 34

She announced in 2025 that she had been diagnosed with cancer.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Ciara Mageean, an Irish runner who set national records in the 800 meters, mile, and 1500 meters, died November 1, according to a social media post from her family. She was 34.

Mageean was diagnosed with stage 4 bowel cancer in May 2025.

She competed in two Olympics, in 2016 and 2021, in the 1500 meters, but she could not race at the Games in 2024, due to an Achilles injury.

The timing of that injury was unfortunate, because from 2023 to early 2024, Mageean was at the height of her powers.

In 2023, she ran personal bests in the mile (4:14.58) in June and 1500 meters (3:55.87) in September. That PR came en route to a victory at the Brussels Diamond League meet. In May of 2024, she ran 1:58.51 for 800 meters and the next month, she won the European Championships 1500 meters. Her final professional race was a Diamond League 2,000 meters in July 2024 in Monaco.

Mageean announced her cancer in a July 2025 post on Instagram, in which only her right arm, hooked up to a tube, was visible. The Olympic rings were tattooed on the inside of her wrist.

In June, Mageean released a book, My Greatest Race, about her cancer diagnosis. It became an all-Ireland bestseller.

Mageean was sponsored by New Balance, and at times, New Balance Boston athletes would cross paths with Mageean during altitude training stints in Flagstaff, Arizona. American miler Elle St. Pierre said she admired how tenacious Mageean was, training hard even when she couldn’t run due to injury.

“She was just very resilient,” St. Pierre said. “Through a number of injuries, she always came back so fast, and I feel like she she handled that mentally really well, too, and she’d still be training. That’s a really tough part of the sport, but something that really that stood out to me.”

Across the elite running world, athletes took to social media to pay tribute to Mageean, who had married Thomas Moran a few weeks ago in Belfast. Mageean posted photos from her wedding on Instagram six days ago.

Mark Coogan, coach of New Balance Boston, remembers enjoying a Guinness after the New Balance Indoor Games and laughing with Mageean.

“I saw her more as as a friend and someone to root for than someone that we were trying to beat all the time,” Coogan said.

Mageean set her mile national record in the race where Faith Kipyegon of Kenya set the world record.

“I will remember Ciara as a lovely person in and out of competition,” Kipyegon wrote on Instagram. “Simply an amazing person. I wish everyone around her strength in these difficult times.”

Síofra Cléirigh Büttner, who also ran for New Balance Boston and competed internationally for Ireland, plans to be in Dublin in December. She had texted Mageean just a few weeks ago to congratulate her on her wedding and suggest they have coffee. Mageean texted back, “I’d love to get coffee.”

Her death, Cléirigh Büttner said, feels sudden.

Mageean was a star from a young age, and instead of going to the U.S. for college and opting to run in the NCAA system, she stayed home in Ireland, with the backing of New Balance, and competed at home.

When Cléirigh Büttner was deciding what to do for college, Mageean came over for dinner one night to listen and offer her advice. “She was always just a very selfless person as well as just such a driven and ambitious and talented athlete,” Cléirigh Büttner said. (She decided to go to Villanova.)

“There was definitely something just very special and genuine about her, both as an athlete and a person.”

Mageean was also one of Ireland’s great sporting heroes, Cléirigh Büttner said.

“I think it will be a long time before the Irish nation is over this loss,” she said.

Sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

#8907. Stop Chain Skipping: How to Adjust Your Rear Derailleur for Smoother, Cleaner Shifts

A step-by-step guide to cleaner shifts on mechanical and electronic rear derailleurs.

Many of us have been there—try to shift and the chain just does not want to get up into that next gear. That frustrating click click click as the chain can’t make the jump is like nails on a chalkboard.

The rear derailleur is a key piece of equipment on the bike—especially with the gaining popularity of single chainring setups. The good news is that adjusting a rear derailleur is a fairly straightforward process.

On bikes with cable-actuated derailleurs keep in mind that as you ride (especially after getting a new bike or a new rear derailleur cable installed) the rear derailleur cable will settle into the bike—you’ll hear shops call this cable stretch. Over time you’ll need to add a little cable tension to the system to make sure your shifting stays tight and crisp.

Below we’ll go through everything from how to do a quick cable tension adjustment to how to spot a bent derailleur hanger so you can keep your shifting smooth for your next ride.

Your rear derailleur moves your chain across cogs and maintains proper tension on the chain with every gear change. How? The chain runs around two jockey pulleys on the rear derailleur. When you shift to a larger chainring or cog, the shifter cable pulls the rear derailleur forward, causing the pulleys to push the chain onto the larger sprockets while keeping chain tension in check.

When you shift to a smaller cog, the shifter cable releases the rear derailleur, which swings outward, taking up chain slack and causing the pulleys to pull the chain onto a smaller sprocket. If everything is set up correctly, your rear derailleur should make one clean shift for every click of your shifter.

Before adjusting anything on the derailleur, first ensure that your rear derailleur hanger is straight. A bent hanger is often the cause of rear derailleur shifting woes.

The derailleur hanger is the part of the frame to which your rear derailleur mounts. Derailleur hangers are made to bend or break under impact and not destroy your expensive frame or drivetrain. On carbon and aluminum frames, this hanger is often replaceable. If bent inward, you can very gently align it. But your best remedy is to have your local shop use a special hanger alignment tool to fix it, or replace the hanger entirely. Universal derailleur hangers have gotten more popular, but different frames need different hangers. Pick up an extra hanger to keep at home, but make sure you have the right one for your bike. This small and relatively inexpensive part will come in handy when you need it in a pinch.

If your chain doesn’t move when you shift, or it skips cogs, your rear derailleur may be out of alignment. Hop off your bike and do this: Shift your chain into the biggest chainring and smallest cog, then loosen the cable clamp bolt (where the cable attaches to the derailleur).

Look for the high and low adjusters on the derailleur—often marked with an H and an L. Adjust the high-gear screw by turning it until the jockey pulleys line up with the smallest cog. Your chain should move smoothly around the cog and pulleys when you turn the pedals.

To check alignment with the largest cog, rotate the pedal forward and push the rear derailleur so that the chain shifts to the largest cog. If the pulleys take the chain beyond the largest cog, screw the low adjuster inward until this stops. Reattach the cable and tighten the clamp.

Fine-tune with the barrel adjuster, located where the cable housing enters the rear derailleur. For the best performance, position the guide pulley roughly 6 to 7 mm away from the cogs. If your chain skips when you shift to a lower gear, give the barrel adjuster a half-turn counterclockwise. (Tip: Think L for lower and for left turn.) A higher gear? Try a half-turn clockwise.

Sometimes the cause of a skipping-feeling of your shifting is a stiff chain link. This happens when one or more chain links doesn’t properly articulate, either from corrosion or damage to the chain. This can be mitigated by cleaning your chain and adding a few drops of lube to each of the rollers and pins. This creates a smooth and efficient chain and allows your rear derailleur to move through the cogs without hesitating. To check for a stiff link, gently backpedal the chain and pay attention to how the chain rolls off the derailleur pulleys. If any links skip, work some lube into the link and gently flex the link until the chain moves smoothly.

Also check your chain for excessive wear—an overly worn chain can also cause poor shifting. As a chain is ridden, the bushings and rollers in the chain wear out, causing slop to develop and the distance between the pin centers to increase. (This is commonly called “chain stretch,” though the metal in the chain hasn’t really stretched.) Generally, when a chain “stretches” by 0.5 percent, it is time to swap the chain.

The easiest way to test for wear is a chain checker tool. But you can also use a ruler. A fresh chain measures 12 inches from pin center to pin center. If it measures more than 12 ¹⁄₁₆ inches, change your chain.

After cleaning, add a few drops of lube to the pivot points. (there are eight) of the parallelogram linkage, cycle through a few shifts, then wipe off any excess lube. When you clean your chain, clear any muck from the inner and outer surfaces of both pulleys—it collects at the base of their teeth. Make sure to wipe away all the excess that may reside on your chain, pulleys, and pivot points.

First, remove the chain. Many chains use some sort of quick removal link to make this easy, so look for that first. If not, break your chain with a chain tool or, if your chain is joined by a connecting pin, by removing the pin (use a new pin to rejoin the chain). Loosen the cable-clamp bolt on the rear derailleur and pull the shifter cable out. Undo the hex bolt that attaches the derailleur hanger from the rear dropout.

Make sure your new derailleur is compatible with your bike’s shifters; eight- through 11-speed shifters must be matched with the same manufacturer’s equivalent derailleur. Attach the new derailleur to the hanger using its hex bolt. Reattach the cable and loop the chain through the jockey wheels before reconnecting the chain. Shift through all gear combinations to make sure everything is running smoothly. If it isn’t, turn the barrel adjuster on the derailleur in or out to fine-tune shifting.

While your electronic rear derailleur operates on the same principles as the mechanical version, the biggest difference is the electronic rear derailleur has a tiny motor doing the work of pushing and pulling rather than a cable. That motor is powered by a battery that sends and receives signals from either a wireless or wired connection to the rear derailleur.

With an electronic system, shifting is managed by firmware, so it shouldn’t go out of alignment once it’s set up—though it may be adjustable through an app or other software tool (and it may need firmware updates). If you’re having trouble with your electronic derailleur, first check to make sure the battery has enough charge. Make sure any cables are fully connected as well.

When electronic derailleurs are shifting poorly, one of the first things I check is the hardware. Bent derailleur cages, hangers, or damaged derailleurs can all cause poor shifting, so assess those parts while your firmware updates.

There are a few important steps to be aware of prior to adjusting or fixing your rear derailleur. Identify which brand of electronic drivetrain is on your bike. Each brand has a different procedure on how to troubleshoot or adjust your rear derailleur.

Once identified, confirm whether it is wired or wireless. Then, double-check that the battery or battery interface is connected or has power. The following steps are unique depending on which brand of drivetrain you have.

Step 1: Charge your battery and check the coin-cell batteries in the shift levers (as basic as this sounds, it’s often the issue when a SRAM AXS or Shimano Di2 drivetrain suddenly stops shifting).

Step 2: Download the manufacturer’s mobile app.

Step 3: Check for any derailleur or shifter firmware updates.

Step 4: Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for derailleur and shifting adjustment (often there are step-by-step instructions in the app or check the brand’s website for details).

#8906. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.
