#8890. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

#8889. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8886. Jess McClain’s Coach—Record-Setting Ultramarathoner David Roche—Shares a Key Training Tactic for Fighting Late-Race Fatigue

This simple long-run tweak can help your legs stay strong when the late miles hit.

Many runners think of the climbs as the toughest part of a hilly race. Uphills send your heart rate soaring and slow even the strongest runners to a grind, while descents offer a chance to catch your breath and let gravity do some of the work. But David Roche, ultramarathoner and coach to New York City Marathon women’s runner-up Jess McClain, says those easier-feeling downhills can come at a cost later in the race.

And Roche knows the importance of late-race performance, which is why he integrates strategies into his training to fight fatigue through long distances.

Take McClain’s finish in New York City as an example: She outkicked reigning champ Hellen Obiri just feet from the finish line to take second place by mere seconds, clocking 2:24:42 and becoming the first American woman to reach the podium in NYC since 2018.

Roche’s fatigue-fighting tactics take him even farther in his own races. The two-time Life Time Leadville 100 winner—and course record holder—covered the famously demanding trails in 15:12:30, averaging roughly 9:07 per mile. Yet he rarely relies on extremely long, arduous training runs to prepare for conquering late miles.

Instead, Roche uses downhill workouts to reproduce some of the muscular stress that can cause runners’ legs to fail in an endurance event. “Downhills are the gateway to fatigue resistance in these really long events,” Roche tells Runner’s World.

The best part is, you don’t have to be an elite like McClain or Roche to benefit from his advice. He shares how purposeful downhill training can help runners preserve their strength, form, and pace deep into a race. Plus, he offers his go-to workout to add to your buildup.

Running downhill may provide some relief to your cardiovascular system—by lowering your heart rate a bit as gravity naturally carries you downward—but it puts much more strain on your musculoskeletal system. To keep you from tumbling down the hill, the quads must repeatedly brake the body’s momentum.

Braking action involves eccentric contractions, meaning the muscles produce force while lengthening under load, Roche explains. Eccentric contractions occur during many activities—including simply walking down stairs—but running a lengthy descent can deliver thousands in succession, significantly increasing the load on your muscles.

When the body isn’t accustomed to the stress caused by downhill running, the aftermath can wreck you. Roche explains that while a runner may feel relatively normal after their first downhill running workout, they end up developing significant soreness within a day or two. “That feeling of, ‘Oh man, I have no quads right now,’ a few days later is also what happens to your quads in an ultra,” Roche says—and even a marathon.

The initial downhill running effort, however, also triggers an adaptation known as the repeated bout effect. A review published in 2024 on the subject describes the repeated bout effect as a form of skeletal-muscle memory in which the first eccentric challenge activates protective responses that make the muscle more resistant to damage than subsequent ones.

Scientists haven’t identified one physiological mechanism that fully explains the effect. Instead, the review suggests several adaptations may work together. The nervous system may distribute the load more effectively across the muscles, while changes to muscle fibers, tendons, and the extracellular matrix—the structural network surrounding the cells—may help the tissue tolerate force. The inflammatory response may also become better regulated after the body has encountered that stress before.

Basically, the more downhill running you do in your training, the less sore your legs will become after each workout, Roche explains. Using the downhill bout effect to your benefit in this way helps keep your legs stronger later in races as they handle similar impact.

Research shows this phenomenon in action: In a study published in 2022, 10 recreational male runners completed the same 30-minute treadmill run at a 20 percent decline twice, with three weeks between sessions. Following the second run, the athletes experienced a smaller rise in creatine kinase—a blood marker commonly used to assess muscle damage following exercise—along with less soreness and a smaller reduction in maximal force. Their running mechanics were also less disrupted after the second session.

The practical takeaway: With the appropriate exposure, the legs can learn to handle downhills with less fallout. That makes downhill training particularly valuable for ultrarunners who spend multiple hours in a race descending hills, but Roche believes the same principle applies to road runners, too.

At mile 20 of your marathon, your limiting factor isn’t always your heart or your lungs. You could simply lack the muscular strength to keep the same mechanics or pace. Downhill running is Roche’s solution to prepare for that problem without requiring immense volume, and his go-to workout is simpler than you might expect.

For most runners, Roche’s downhill workout isn’t a complicated interval session. It’s an easy long run with a deliberate change in pace when you reach a decline. Roche uses variations of this downhill workout twice per week in his own training, recommending most athletes start with one session and progress from there based on how they recover.

“Because the aerobic demand [of the run] is low, it’s just about pushing the steeper terrain in a way that causes eccentric muscle contractions,” Roche says.

Instead of trying to stack as many miles as possible to mimic race-day conditions, Roche recommends runners focus race-day muscular demand into a 16-mile effort. The faster descents repeatedly load the quads, while the surrounding easy running provides the aerobic work that’s crucial for long-distance racing, says Roche.

According to Roche, in an ideal scenario, you should aim for downhills as steep as—or steeper than—those in your goal race. Running these downhills faster than your race pace ensures your muscles can take on the challenges your goal race will present.

While Roche’s recommended 16-mile run is generally reserved for experienced athletes preparing for marathons or longer, you can scale the same principle to nearly any experience level or race distance by shortening the overall run.

The purpose of downhill training isn’t to leave the quads wrecked every week. Initial sessions may cause soreness, but over time, the same type of descent should become less disruptive, allowing you to recover more easily and withstand greater late-race fatigue.

The workout succeeds not because of how much punishment the quads absorb during one run, but because they’re still capable of working when the race delivers the same punishment as you approach the finish line.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#8885. The Lat Training Guide For Building a Stronger and Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Most lifters want lats for one reason:  the V-taper. Well-developed lats give your upper body that powerful look from the front, side, and back, and yes, they make T-shirts fit better.

Besides looking awesome, the lats keep your shoulders stable, support better upper-body posture, and connect your arms to your torso, improving form during heavy lifts. Strong lats improve pulling mechanics, create a stronger pressing setup, and help your upper back stay in a better position during squats and deadlifts.

Here we’ll go over all things lats, including:

By the end, you’ll know how to train your lats for a stronger back, better pulls, healthier shoulders, and an upper body that will fill out your T-shirts.

The latissimus dorsi—or lats for short—are the body’s widest muscles and cover much of the back. They’re broad, flat, and fan-shaped, which is why well-developed lats help create that V-Taper look.

Because of their size, the lats attach to the

Because they attach to the upper arm and spine, they influence both shoulder movement and posture.

They also help with scapular depression, which pulls the shoulders down away from your ears and is an important part of good pulling form. Train those actions well, and you’ll build a wider back, stronger pulls, and better control from your shoulders through your hips.

We all know that lats are the engine behind rows, pull-ups, and chin-ups, but some don’t realize the vital role they play beyond them.

During the deadlift, strong, engaged lats help keep the bar close to your body as you pull. When the bar drifts away, the lift gets harder, and your lower back gets unhappy.

Your lats matter during the bench press, too. When engaged, they help create a stable base to press from, improve your pressing path, and transfer force from your leg drive to your upper body.

That is why strong lats aren’t just a “back day” thing: they set the table for better pressing form.

Pulling your lats down and back creates upper-body tightness for barbell back squat. Doing so helps stabilize the bar and keeps you in a stronger, more upright position instead of folding forward into a good morning.

The lats also matter for shoulder health and posture because they influence shoulder position and upper-body alignment. When the lats are balanced in length, they let the shoulder blades rest flat, and the shoulders open back naturally. This supports better posture.

And yes, they matter outside the gym, too. Pulling open heavy doors, climbing, carrying objects close to your body, and lifting things from the floor all involve the lats. Bigger lats create the look, but stronger lats help you pull, brace, carry, and move well.

Because the lats are large and their muscle fibers run in different directions, train them through several pulling paths. You need vertical pulling, horizontal pulling, straight-arm work, loaded stretches, and good form to keep the tension where it belongs.

You know the exercises, but that’s only part of it. For maximum growth and strength, keep these four things in mind.

Progressive Overload: Add load, reps, sets, range of motion, or better control over time. But don’t sacrifice lat tension, shoulder position, or form to move more weight.

Here are general recommendations that work for most lifters most of the time.

Use sets of three to six reps on heavier pulls. Good options include weighted pull-ups, heavy chin-ups, and lat pulldowns. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between sets, and keep the reps clean.

Use sets of eight to 15 reps on pulldowns, rows, dumbbell rows to the hip, seated machine rows, or cable rows. This is your bread-and-butter hypertrophy work. Use a full range of motion, control the stretch, and finish each rep by pulling the elbows toward the ribs or hips, depending on the exercise.

Use sets of 12 to 20 reps on straight-arm pulldowns, kneeling straight-arm pulldowns, cable pullovers, and band straight-arm pulldowns. These are great for lifters who struggle to feel their lats because these exercises isolate them.

Straight-arm pulldown variations are useful before deadlifting because engaging the lats helps maintain a neutral spine and keep the bar close. One or two sets of 10 to 15 reps work well as a primer.

Most lifters can train the lats directly two to three times per week.

Think of 12 to 16 direct lat sets per week as your weekly target. How you divide those sets depends on your goal.

If strength is the priority, spend more sets in the 3 to 6 rep range with weighted pull-ups, heavy pulldowns, chin-ups, and rows. If size is the goal, focus more work in the 8 to 15 rep range with pulldowns, rows, single-arm work, and machine or cable variations. If you struggle to feel your lats, include 12 to 20 rep sets of straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers, or band work.

Here’s an example of how to organize your weekly volume. 12 weekly sets might include four heavier sets, six muscle-building sets, and two higher-rep straight-arm sets. That gives you a fantastic combination of strength, size, and lat connection.

Using too much weight you cannot control might stroke the ego, but it does nothing for your gains. Here are a few more mistakes to watch out for to get the most out of your lat training.

Your hands hold the bar, but your elbows should lead the movement. When lifters focus only on pulling with their hands, chin-ups, pulldowns, and rows often turn into biceps-heavy exercises with a side order of forearm fatigue.

Fix: Drive your elbows down during pulldowns, pull your elbows toward your hips during rows, and tuck your shoulder blades into your back pocket for chin-ups.

Many lifters cut the top of pulldowns, pull-ups, and straight-arm exercises short. That leaves a lot of potential lat tension on the table, because the lats love a loaded stretch.

Fix: Reach overhead or forward under control, keep the ribs down, and feel the stretch without dumping on the shoulder joint. The goal is to control a stretch, not just hang through the connective tissue.

When the ribs flare, the lower back often arches, turning a lat exercise into a lower-back exercise. This can happen during pulldowns, pullovers, and straight-arm work when someone tries to create range they don’t own.

Fix: Keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis by breathing out and bracing the core on top of that. This gives the lats a better chance to lengthen and shorten without the lower back taking over.

If your shoulders shrug toward your ears during rows or pulldowns, your upper traps dominate. Doing so takes the focus off the lats and can lead to upper trap and neck pain.

Fix: Remember to keep your shoulders away from your ears and your chest up. You do this by keeping your neck long.

Lat training has its share of gym myths because everyone wants a wider back. Some advice sounds good until you realize it ignores range of motion, elbow path, body position, and the fact that your biceps will love to steal the show if you let them.

Wide-grip pulldowns and pull-ups are great, but they aren’t magic—and they don’t build wide lats. A wide grip doesn’t automatically increase lat tension. In fact, it often shortens your range of motion, limits the load, and shifts stress to the shoulders and upper back for many lifters. Shoulder-width, medium, and neutral grips offer a longer ROM, and you can lift more weight.

Pull-ups and chin-ups are gold-standard lat builders—but the lats need more. The problem is that pull-ups lock you into a single line of pull. Because the lats are large and wide, with muscle fibers running in different directions, dumbbell and machine variations let you adjust your body position and grips to change the line of pull and target muscle fibers that chin-ups miss.

Rows hammer the upper back, but they can also hit the lats with the right setup, grip, and elbow path. Rowing high with flared elbows shifts more attention to the traps, rear delts, and upper back. Rowing back toward the hip with your elbow close gives the lats more work.

They assist with deadlifts, squats, bench press setup, posture, and shoulder control. So yes, train them for width. But don’t forget they also help you lift better when no one is admiring your V-taper.

The lats don’t need a separate “back day or bust” approach. You can train them hard during an upper-body session or weave them into a full-body workout.

Goal: Build lat size and strength while still training the chest, shoulders, upper back, and arms.

Goal: Train the lats as part of a full-body workout.

The winning formula is this: Train the lats with vertical pulls, rows, straight-arm work, single-arm variations, and exercises that challenge the stretch position. Keep the ribs down, control the shoulders, pull toward the hips to engage more lats, and stop letting your biceps, traps, and lower back take over.

Remember to lock the lats in during your squat, bench, and deadlift because they are the difference between a sloppy rep and a clean one. Use enough volume to grow and enough weight to build muscle and strength, but never shortchange the range of motion.

If you do it right, you’ll need to buy larger shirts.

#8884. Dragon Pose Is the Essential Recovery Stretch For Tight Hips and Back

The yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

The low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Log into your Iberia Plus account and search for business class award flights on your target dates. Look for flights priced at 34,000 Avios one-way. If availability is not showing, try shifting dates by 1-2 days within the off-peak window.

Once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

Complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

#8879. I Rode My Bike in a Climate Chamber That Can Recreate Almost Any Weather on the Planet—Here’s My Biggest Takeaway

Inside Italy’s Terra X Cube, a Tour de France simulation became a real-world heat test.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I looked into the giant chamber filled with strategically placed bike trainers and couldn’t help but question what I signed up for. The chamber we were walking into is called the Terra X Cube located in Bolzano, Italy, and is designed to replicate conditions from anywhere on the planet. The chamber can recreate a snowstorm on Mount Everest or a heat wave in the Sahara.

Variables like temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, and altitude can all be controlled from a small observation room just one door over. I knew immediately when I crossed into the threshold of the chamber and the heat hit me in the face that this would be a rough trainer ride.

I was in Bolzano, Italy for an opportunity to participate in this testing in the Terra X Cube as well as tour the apparel brand Q36.5’s headquarters based in Bolzano. The apparel from Q36.5 quickly became my top choice for cycling apparel after getting the chance to test some pieces from their kit for the last few months. Our hot and humid summer in the Northeast gave a perfect testing ground for the Q36.5 Dottore jersey and bibs—and they shined. When a chance to learn more about this brand by visiting their Italian headquarters came up, I jumped on a plane—the opportunity to experience riding in a climate chamber was a special bonus.

Here I’m going to talk about the unique experience of riding in a climate chamber with the heat turned up and my biggest takeaway that you can apply to your trainer riding this season.

The test course and climate were designed to replicate the last section of Stage 2 from the 2026 men’s Tour de France ending in Barcelona. We rode with a custom workout in Zwift and our data was being tracked across the board: SRM cranks to track power, heart rate data to validate fatigue, and CORE sensors to track our heat strain throughout the workout. The room was set to a balmy 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

There was even a tester from Q36.5 in the room with us with a custom jersey. The jersey he wore was effectively two jerseys cut in half at the zipper and straight down the back. He had multiple CORE heat sensors attached around his body to track which jersey design and material was more effective at thermoregulation. One of those jersey designs will end up in a future product.

The ride was supposed to last for about 45 minutes, but our group was the first of the day and ran into some technical difficulties getting the trainers set up. In one sense this was good because we were able to have an extended warmup on the trainers, but the reality meant we spent an extra 45 minutes warming up in the already heated up chamber.

Thankfully, over the last few months, I’ve been doing heat training protocols with my CORE training sensor. I dove straight in with six weeks of active heat training, then I pivoted to strictly passive heat training with my home sauna. While I was absolutely heating up I was relatively comfortable rolling into the ride.

Once we got through our extended warmup we began the proper ride. Effectively we were shooting for an over-under workout that emulated the end of stage two at this year’s Tour de France. I had my CORE temperature data up on the screen and saw that before we were starting the ride my internal temperature was at about 99 degrees. The giant fans at the front of the room would change power to replicate the airflow during climbs versus descents, but at those temperatures it felt like sitting in front of a massive hair dryer.

As we began the official warmup my temperature steadily climbed—according to my CORE sensor I peaked just over 102 degrees. In the middle of the test I looked around the room and everyone looked like they were putting out high effort, even when we were supposed to be sitting in our recovery phase. The heat was taking its toll and our views did not inspire a boost in energy. Staring at the metallic walls while pedaling on our hamster wheel bikes did not give inspiration for an extra push for our final sprint. But as we finished up our not-so-cool cooldown I couldn’t help but think I would do it again.

After our group left the chamber the second group queued up for their turn on the bikes. The technical difficulties were overcome with our group, so they were able to jump straight into the ride after a five-minute warmup. That night we all regrouped to go through the data and we were able to see our data versus the data from some of the professionals in the stage we recreated. My biggest takeaway from the comparison to the professionals was their core temperature data. The professionals we were comparing against showed very little heat strain compared to even the fittest in our group. It’s worth noting the professionals had also already ridden over 60 miles before our route even started—those professionals were extremely heat adapted.

My biggest personal takeaway was how I could recreate this at home. When I talked to someone else in my group we discussed the similarities to this experience and heat training at home. When I do an active heat session at home I layer up in three layers top and bottom, a painter’s suit with the shins and feet cut off (so it doesn’t get caught in the cranks), and a hat or beanie for good measure. My active heat session numbers at home are surprisingly similar to this experience: typically a 45-minute warmup gets me into zone three of the heat strain index in the CORE app and then I spend about 45 minutes in this zone. This shows you don’t need a massive climate chamber to get the training benefits of heat training. Some warm layers, a painter’s suit, a CORE sensor, and a bike trainer can give you the benefits you need to develop this component of training.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There was a time when eight miles felt like an eternity to Weini Kelati. Now, toward the tail end of preparing for her first full marathon, she can find herself 10 miles into a 20-mile workout and realize the distance that once signaled the end of a hard day has now become the halfway point.

This progression says a lot about what marathon preparation requires. The obvious difference between a half marathon and 26.2 miles is distance, but Kelati discovered that building a marathon body involved more than adding more miles to her workload. The body must be conditioned to tolerate additional volume, know how to fuel, how to recover, and eventually trust that the work was enough when fatigue arrives.

Kelati, the American half-marathon record holder, Olympian, and five-time national champion will make her marathon debut at the TCS New York City Marathon on Nov. 1. Speaking with Muscle & Fitness through New York Road Runners, she explained that she had always seen the half marathon as a gateway toward eventually racing 26.2, even giving herself a loose requirement of completing four or five before considering making the move.

“I think first I was nervous,” Kelati said. “I was like, ‘Oh my goodness. This is going to be hard because I used to be at low mileage.’”

What surprised her most isn’t how difficult the transition was, but how quickly the human body can begin adjusting to something once intimidating as simply another day in training.

During Kelati’s half-marathon preparation, she said her highest weekly mileage reached around 75 miles. For this build, she knew that number would have to climb into the 90s. The increase initially made her nervous. Once she started, however, something unexpected happened: She began enjoying it.

The biggest adjustment was redefining what constitutes a long effort. In the lead-up to a 10K or half-marathon, a six- or eight-mile tempo run could represent one of the bigger sustained sessions on her schedule. Marathon preparation introduced two different types of long runs, including easier road efforts and workouts, which she can cover approximately 20 miles at a specific pace.

“I’m not the type of person who rushes into something,” Kelati said. “I always take a lot baby steps to get used to something.”

That patience allowed her body to establish a new baseline without making every unfamiliar distance feel like a test. Her weekly structure wasn’t radically different from half-marathon training, either. The biggest change is that familiar paces and workouts extended further, asking her to sustain what she already knew for considerably longer.

The result was a changed internal relationship with distance.

“When you get to eight miles, you start saying, ‘Oh, I’m already halfway,’ instead of saying, ‘Oh, I used to stop here,” Kelati says. “The mind and the body change the way I have to handle it.”

The added mileage exposed an area Kelati admits hasn’t always been a strength for her: nutrition.

At shorter distances, she could get away with habits that weren’t conducive with marathon preparation. For years, she could wake up and run without eating anything because consuming food before a morning session wasn’t something she enjoyed.

The marathon build forced her to adjust that part of her routine. When there is a large increase in workload, personal preferences eventually run into physical necessity.

“You have to help the body as much as it’s working,” Kelati said. “During the marathon training, you have to fuel your body. You have to get ready for the next hard run.”

She learned that fueling for her bigger sessions didn’t mean forcing down a huge meal. If appetite was an issue, she would have smaller meals spaced throughout the day. This same logic changed her behavior after a run.

Meals were the common recovery method for Kelati,  but the increased workload led her to incorporate recovery drinks and pay closer attention to getting nutrition back into her body sooner.

Kelati’s favorite recovery method didn’t require scheduling or involve any expensive equipment.

“I love taking naps after every single run,” she said. “It doesn’t matter how hard or easy the run I do, I just have to take a little nap every day and, of course, more than eight hours of sleep during the night.”

Kelati fully believes giving her body adequate downtime has been an important reason she was able to absorb demanding training and be able to show up the following morning and ask her body to perform again.

There is one part of marathon preparation Kelati couldn’t completely simulate.

She could run 20 miles in training, nap after training, and ask experienced marathoners what waits beyond the distances she already knows.

Until New York, however, she won’t know exactly how her own body and mind will respond to racing 26.2 miles. That uncertainty doesn’t seem to bother her as much as thinking about the entire distance at once.

“I don’t like counting the miles,” Kelati said. “It seems pretty long for me to think about it while you’re standing on the start line or you just started. You’re in the first mile, and you’re just like, ‘Oh, we have like 25 miles to go.’”

Instead, she intends on remaining completely in the moment.

“I just like to be in the present and focus one mile at a time,” she said.

Insights have helped. Kelati did the same thing before moving into half marathons, quizzing runners about which points of the race are the most challenging so she could have some idea of what awaited her. This time, the answer is a different number.

“They keep saying, ‘You’re going to start racing when you get to 30K,’” she says. “It can be different, but also it’ll give you what to expect or what’s coming when you get to that distance and how you’re going to handle it.”

Discomfort will eventually arrive, and Kelati’s strategy is a simple one. She reminds herself that the pain is temporary and that she’d rather find out what she’s capable of than finish wondering whether she would have given more.

It’s a mindset that comes from weeks of watching her body handle workloads she once was uncertain about. Kelati says one of the things she’s most proud of during this build has been how naturally she adapted to the training her coach put in front of her. Each completed run and training session has chipped away the stone of uncertainty that existed when 26.2 was still just a thought.

“When you try to do something new, you always have these thoughts that can prevent you from doing something,” Kelati said. “But then once you just start doing it, I feel like we can do anything when we believe.”

When Kelati reaches the start line in Staten Island, there will be lots of thoughts in her head. All the early morning runs, how well she’s done in races in New York, and all the months spent gradually extending what her body can tolerate.

She will let those thoughts flow. Her goal for that morning speaks to her readiness.

“I want to feel good just standing there and say, ‘Today is a great day,’” Kelati said. ‘“I feel good. Let’s do this.’”
